Yesterday the right hon.
leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) asked

a question with respect to the alleged lack of feed for live stock and the need of relief experienced by farmers at Ravenscrag, Saskatchewan. The answer to my right hon. friend's question is that, following the receipt of complaint by the dominion Department of Agriculture from Ravenscrag, Saskatchewan, it has been ascertained that six hundred and twenty tons of fodder have been delivered to the local improvement district in which Ravenscrag is located, and the one adjacent to the north to which deliveries have been made from Ravenscrag. Three carloads have been delivered to date to Ravenscrag in the month of February and one hundred and forty tons are on order for delivery to that point.
Complaint received on February 17 from Ravenscrag by the government of Saskatchewan, by whom the fodder is distributed, was signed by farmers who did not reduce their live stock to the basis on which feed is being supplied, when given an opportunity to do so with assistance from the dominion government.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934, to make provision for the establishment of more than one board of review in any province, to provide that no new proposals shall be filed in a province after a date to be fixed by proclamation, more adequately to define the meaning of the word "creditor" as used in the act, and to extend the benefit of the act in the case of deceased farmers.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston (Lake Centre) in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I had better outline briefly the amendments which are contemplated by the bill which will be based upon this resolution. In doing so, I do not want to anticipate the detailed discussion on the bill itself but to give, so far as I can, general information. A number of members advised me last night that they would be unable to be here to-day but would like to be present when there is any general discussion of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and in that regard I would point out that there will be opportunity for general discussion both on the second reading of the bill itself and in committee of the whole on the bill. At this time I shall content myself with a brief outline of the nature of the proposed amendments and the reasons therefor.
The bill will seek to amend the act in five important respects. The first amendment will attempt to define more adequately the word " creditor," so as to include as a creditor of a farmer a person holding a mortgage, hypothec or other charge upon the property of the farmer even though no privity of contract exists between the farmer and such person. The practice of the boards of review in the various provinces in dealing with cases in which there is no privity of contract has varied quite considerably. Recently, however, certain decisions, particularly one by the appeal court of the province of Ontario, have made it necessary to have a clarifying amendment, which will now make it clear that the word "creditor" does include the creditor of a farmer, although no privity of contract exists between that creditor and the farmer, because of the fact that he is a mortgagee of a previous owner of the property.
The second amendment is designed to permit the legal representative of a deceased farmer to
apply to the court for an order to continue proceedings under a proposal filed by the farmer before his death or for leave to make a proposal on behalf of the estate of a deceased farmer, and the court would be empowered to grant the necessary application upon being satisfied that a member of the family of the deceased farmer resides, and will continue to reside, upon the farm, and intends and is able to operate the farm.
The third amendment is intended to change the present provision which provides that a stay of proceedings is effective only for ninety days, subject to extension by order of the court. Where a delay in hearing the case occurs the official receiver has to apply to the court within ninety days for an extension of the order, and in some cases many extensions have had to be obtained. The new provision will make the stay of proceedings effective until the proposal is finally disposed of. Any creditor, however, may in the interim apply to the court for an order to proceed should circumstances develop justifying such action.
The fourth amendment proposed will enable the governor in council to appoint more than one board of review in a province. In some provinces the number of cases referred to the board has been so great that the boards have not been able to keep up to date with the work. It is not anticipated that action will be taken in all provinces under this amendment or that action will be taken except under circumstances which indicate that such is absolutely necessary in order to catch up with the work and clear it up.
The fifth amendment will enable the governor in council by proclamation to provide that no proposal shall be filed in any province after a date fixed in such proclamation. This amendment is in order to enable the government to meet the very varied conditions which exist in Canada with respect to the operation of this act.
Strong representations have been made from some of the provinces that the operation of the act is no longer beneficial but rather harmful to farmers in that the conditions which gave rise to its enactment and its operation in the province, have now sufficiently improved that there is no need for it; and representations are also made that the fact that it does continue to operate under such circumstances has an impairing effect upon the credit of farmers. The government desires to be in a position to treat each province according to the circumstances of the farmers in that province. By providing that the act should cease to operate, that no new applications will be accepted after a certain date, the same method is followed as was adopted in bringing the act into force. It is hoped
Farmers' Creditors Act

that the amendment will relieve the government of a great volume of requests from some provinces for the complete repeal of the whole statute, because the government have no doubt that the statute is still a necessary instrument in certain provinces. The intention is to keep it in operation in every province so long as real need for it is demonstrated. But the government is definitely of opinion also that the continuance in operation of this piece of machinery within a province after the need for it has vanished tends to lower the credit of the agricultural industry in that province, which is to say the least an undesirable result.
That, Mr. Chairman, is a brief explanation of the purpose of the amendments which will be covered by the bill to which this resolution is a preliminary. On the second reading of the bill and in committee I shall have available all possible information with respect to the operation of the act. As I stated at the outset, a number of hon. members on both sides who are not here to-day have asked to be given an opportunity to get such information from me, and I can undertake to be in a position, if not to answer all questions, at least to supply such information as I have on every aspect of the matter when we come to the further stage.

maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the amendments proposed by the minister are twofold. Taking the latter one first, I heartily approve of it on the grounds he has put forward. During the past two years I have had many interviews with farmers who felt that the act was detrimental to them in that they did not come under the act but desired to borrow money and found the act a serious obstacle to their doing so. For that reason they advocated repeal. I had proposed and in fact had drafted a bill to present to this house which differs from what the minister has outlined in only one respect: I was going to suggest July 1, 1938, as a suitable date for the repeal of the act in Ontario. I admit at once that the minister may be in a better position to judge when the repeal in any province should become effective, but I think the date I mentioned is a reasonable one for Ontario. It is to be borne in mind that this act has no application to a debt incurred after the enactment of the legislation in 1934, over three years ago. The act of course is based upon the assumption that the farmer is insolvent; that is the fundamental requirement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: That his business as a farmer is insolvent. That has an important bearing on some suggestions.

maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not quite get the distinction, but there may be one in the mind of the minister. If a man's business is bankrupt it seems that he is bankrupt himself. However, the act is based upon that assumption; unless that situation exists the act has no application. Bearing in mind that the act came into effect in 1934, surely the farmer to whom it was intended to apply must have found out by this time whether or not he is insolvent in respect of his liabilities prior to
1934.	So it seems to me that a reasonable time has elapsed, having in mind the object of the legislation, which was of a temporary nature, designed to keep farmers on the farm rather than have them sold out and everything cleaned up, even the creditors getting very little out of it. Keeping these facts in mind I believe it is the general feeling that we may well terminate this legislation in Ontario. I have had many communications with farmers about it. True, I have had some representations to the contrary, but they are not nearly as numerous or as convincing as those in favour of terminating the operation of the act.
As to the other amendment, the act of course is based on the assumption that there is a relation of debtor and creditor. A farmer who acquires a farm subject to a mortgage to which he is not a party does not occupy the position of a debtor to the party who holds the mortgage. On that ground I think the minister will agree that the relation is not that of debtor and creditor, and the act has been interpreted as having no application to cases of the kind. I can see some difficulty if this amendment is made. Take the case of a farmer who purchased a farm at a high price shortly after the war when prices were high. He paid a substantial amount of his purchase price, perhaps paid it down cash, giving a mortgage for the balance. The relation of debtor and creditor undoubtedly existed between the purchaser and vendor in that case. But another man comes along and acquires this farm on quite a different basis. It may be fair that as between the original parties to the transaction the debt should be cut down, and it may not be at all fair that as between the last purchaser and the original mortgagee it should be cut down. There is a difference there.
As to proceedings instituted by a farmer now deceased, I have had several cases of that kind, and I am glad the minister proposes to limit the amendment to cases in which say a son or heir of the deceased is staying on the farm. That conforms to the spirit of the act. I think the minister will agree it would be quite proper to say the original intention of the act does not apply where an

Farmers' Creditors Act
estate is being wound up and none of the heirs or parties interested are going to stay on the farm.
Reserving the right to make any further comments when the bill comes down and we know its exact language, I think it is along the right lines. But I again press the minister to consider the first day of July, the national birthday, as the time for termination in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: I hope I made it clear that the intention is to set a date within a province after which no new applications can be received, but the act will continue to operate in that province pending the disposition of cases concerning which application was received prior to the date set in the proclamation. It is felt that examination should be made before definitely determining the date, but my hon. friend's suggestion is not far from my own view as to what it should be in Ontario.

maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: I quite agree with that. It was my intention to make it clear that the wording of the bill I intended to introduce was exactly along that line, that no new applications should be received after the first of July. Of course all those pending, of which there are a large number, should be cleaned up, which will take possibly a year.

maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: Will it be permissible to insert further amendments when the matter is being discussed later in this session in committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: It is an amending bill, of course, and when the bill is in committee of the whole house the whole act is before the committee. At that stage it is quite permissible for anyone to suggest an amendment, provided that it does not involve a charge upon the revenues of the crown or create a tax; this cannot be done unless it is preceded by a resolution such as the one now under consideration. But ordinary amendments of course can be proposed during the committee stage of the bill.

maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the government is to be commended for bringing down amendments to the act at this time. The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act has operated now fairly successfully for almost four years, but the circumstances that prevailed at the time the act was passed do not still exist. While in some provinces the need for the act may be growing less, in others there is need for an expansion of the scope of the act.
I do not propose to go into the conditions in other provinces, in this regard, because I am not familiar with them, but with reference to the province of Saskatchewan'-and I think other members from that province would agree with me-the administration of the act has been received very favourably, and there is a widespread desire on all sides that the scope of the act should be expanded. At the annual meeting of the Canadian Chamber of Agriculture in this city on the 27th day of January, in the course of his speech Mr. J. H. Wesson, the president, outlined four suggested amendments that he thought would be in the interests of agriculture, particularly in Saskatchewan. I do not think it is necessary for me to take the time to read those amendments; no doubt the minister is familiar with them, and, if I may judge from his remarks, they are being included in the bill that is to be brought down. I point that out to show that all sections of opinion in Saskatchewan, including the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, the wheat pool, agricultural societies and so on, recognize the service that this act has been to the farmer and are asking for an extension of its scope. I have before me a resolution which was passed unanimously by the legislature of Saskatchewan last year. So rarely does a resolution pass unanimously in the legislature of that province that in itself that fact makes it worthy of note. All parties agreed on the following resolution:
That the legislature of the province of Saskatchewan, while deeply sensible of the great assistance rendered to our people by the provisions of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in the solution of their financial difficulties occasioned by the present depression, aggravated by unprecedented drought in our most productive areas, are of the opinion that experience of the working of the said act in our province renders desirable amendments thereto whereby it may be provided:
Then it lists them:
(1)	That personal representatives of the estates of deceased persons may he permitted to take advantage of the provisions of the said act as fully as such deceased person could do if alive.
(2)	That the board of review be given power to rehear and amend proposals formulated prior to the 1st of December, 1936.
(3) That the scope of the said act be widened to permit of real property owners in cities, towns, villages and hamlets making proposals under the act to obtain adjustment of mortgages, agreements for sale, liens and other encumbrances on their real property.
(4)	That, where default has been made in performance of the terms of a proposal previously formulated through circumstances not within the control of the debtor, the board of review may prohibit bankruptcy proceedings being taken against him and may make such further or other order as the circumstances of the case warrant.
Farmers' Creditors Act

(5)	That the provisions of the act be extended to make it applicable to retail merchants and traders so as to enable them to claim the benefit of the act.
(6) That the province of Saskatchewan be divided for the purposes of administration of the act into a sufficient number of areas with boards of review to expeditiously carry out the work of debt adjustment under the supervision of the present chairman.
(7)	That, where lands are subject to a registered mortgage or mortgages and the registered owner of the said lands is a farmer who is not a party to each of the said mortgages, such farmer shall be considered a debtor in respect to all the said mortgages and entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, and the board of review may make such order as it deems just and proper, both with respect to the said registered owner and his liability in respect to the said mortgages, and with respect to any mortgagor or mortgagors in the said mortgages and the mortgagor's liability in respect to the said mortgages.
(8)	That the provisions of the act be extended to make it apply to cases where an owner of a farm has sold or leased his farm and given possession to the purchaser or tenant, as the case may be.
And, further, that this legislature urges that amendments to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, embodying the proposed changes, be promulgated at the present session of the federal parliament.
This resolution was adopted unanimously on March 2, 1937. The lawyer members of that house who drew it up must have had their tongues in their cheeks, since even to me-and I am not a lawyer-some of the suggestions it contains would appear to be outside the scope of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and would come rather within the Bankruptcy Act. Nevertheless it indicates that there is a widespread desire in that province, at least, for the retention of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and the extension of its activities.
I want to say just a word with reference to the five amendments that have been outlined by the minister. At the present moment I have on the order paper a bill in this connection, and I am very glad that everything contained in that bill, with two or three exceptions, will be found in the government's legislation. The amendment permitting the estate of deceased farmers to come under the protection of this act in my opinion is a move in the right direction. The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was found to be intra vires because of the fact that it dealt with insolvency, which under section 92 of the British North America Act is within the jurisdiction of the federal government. It would therefore seem that the insolvency of the estate of the deceased farmer ought to have the same right to come, and should come, under this act.

Then I think the amendment to subsection 1 of section 11, to extend the stay of proceedings until the proposals shall have been settled, is also a move in the right direction. In Saskatchewan, because of the volume of applications, the boards of review have been running about a year behind, and when application for a stay of proceedings had to be made every ninety days it occasioned considerable unnecessary work. I think the minister is doing the right thing in making this amendment.
The question of privity of contract has become a problem only recently, and has not yet affected us in Saskatchewan, though undoubtedly it will, in view of the decision of the Ontario supreme court in the now famous Gofton v. Shantz case, in which the following decision was given:
A purchaser of mortgaged property who has not covenanted to pay the mortgage debt is not a debtor of the mortgagee and therefore not entitled to an adjustment of the debt under the provisions of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act; there being no relationship of debtor and creditor, secured or otherwise, between such purchaser and the mortgagee, a proposal under the statute made by the purchaser is not binding on the mortgagee and will have no effect upon the final foreclosure order made in the action to foreclose the mortgage.
From what I can gather from the study of statistics given by the minister's department, in returns from questions asked last year, that would affect a great many hundreds of cases which have been settled in the belief that there was a privity of contract and-
Mr. DUNNING; Thousands of them, probably.

maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, I believe it would run into thousands. I was being conservative by confining it to hundreds. I think an amendment along this line will save a great deal of chaos in regard to that situation.
The suggestion that we have more than one board has been asked for repeatedly by different bodies from Saskatchewan. I notice in an answer to a question I received the other day from the minister that in Saskatchewan 1,116 cases are awaiting the attention of the board of review, and that is the situation at a time when conditions are so bad that people are not bothering about seeking any debt-protecting legislation. Should we have a crop this summer and creditors begin to press their claims, in my opinion the volume of people asking for protection under the act will be doubled or trebled. Certainly there is a need for at least two boards, one to work out of Regina and the other out of Saskatoon.
I come now to the fifth suggestion by the minister-and I am not so directly concerned

Farmers' Creditors Act
with it, because it is inserted in the interest of provinces where the act is not working as suitably. Perhaps I should be more correct if I said that need for the act is not as pressing as it is in the province from which I come. There is only one thing about which I should like to be clear, and undoubtedly the minister will clarify the point when the bill comes up.
I should like to know how it will be decided in each province whether or not the people in that province want a cessation of the activities of the board of review. I should like to know whether a vote of the legislature will cause an announcement to be made that no further applications will be received, or whether some other method will be taken. I hope some safeguard will be taken to see to it that in a province, like Saskatchewan for instance, the good work that has been done and that can be done will not be stopped by any premature cessation of the activities of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act administration.
Before I take my seat I should like to suggest one or two things the minister has not outlined, and which he may be willing to consider between now and the time the bill is presented to the committee. I have in mind the interests of the retired farmer. The minister and every other hon. member from the west knows that in every small town and village there are numbers of people who have left their farms and have been living in the small towns. They have expected to live for the rest of their days upon the proceeds from the farms they have leased. They now find that under the definition of the term "farmer" as it appears in paragraph (f) in section 2 of the bill, they are not farmers, because they are not persons engaged "in the tillage of the soil." For that reason they are not in a position to ask for a reduction of their debts, or that a proposal be formulated between them and their creditors. The result is that in many cases they are continuing to pay heavy interest, and to meet debts which are now out of all proportion to the value of their property. I know that in very many cases they are in the serious position of being in danger of losing their properties.
In some cases these people are in a position which is almost worse than that of the actual farmer on the farm. The farmers have the ordinary means of subsistence, but these people have not. Their only source of revenue has gone. During the last few years their farms have produced nothing, and they are now in the position where they are expected to pay taxes and interest on their
debts, despite the fact that they have no income and have no way of obtaining a settlement with their creditors, through the act.
I wondered if the minister might consider, between now and second reading of the bill the possibility of accepting an amendment which would extend the definition of the term "farmer" to a person who was the owner of a farm, but who had rented or leased it, and whose main source of revenue was to be derived therefrom. I have in mind the positions of those who appeared before the first board of review that was set up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Has the hon. member
given any consideration to that other retired farmer, the one who has not his farm leased under the circumstances outlined by the hon. member but has sold the farm subject to mortgage and is in a position of a creditor under the act? Some of the most heartrending letters I get with respect to the administration of the act are not from debtors. Debtors are being protected by the operation of the act. I am just as sympathetic with the retired farmer who is a creditor and is trying to live honestly on the proceeds of what is owing to him as I am with the debtor retired farmer described by the hon. member. The difficulty with respect to the act is that we tend to look at it from one standpoint only.
I could not refrain from interjecting these observations, because they bear so completely upon what the hon. member was saying. The next door neighbour might be in exactly the opposite position, but there would be no mercy for him; he gets nothing. That is one of the great difficulties of this legislation.

maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am glad the minister has brought that up, because I am aware of the problem of the retired farmer who is a creditor. Bu.t the reason I am emphasizing the case of the debtor retired farmer is that the creditor retired farmer is not primarily a problem which faces us in Saskatchewan. I believe that is one more common to the east.
Mr. DUNNING; But it is a problem under the act.

maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Oh, yes; it is a problem under the act. But I am presenting suggested amendments, in view of the problems, particularly of the people on the prairies. The Saskatchewan brief presented before the Rowell commission showed, for instance, that 83-5 per cent of our farm debt was owing outside the province. In the main it is not owing

maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
For once I agree wholeheartedly with what has been said by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was presented to the house some years ago as offering the best method available at the moment of dealing with the accumulated debts of our farmers. I voted for that act because I believed it was the best we could do at the time. I believe the act has operated for the good of all concerned as applied to farmers who bought land at high prices in 1928 and 1929, or perhaps before that during the war, and had not been able to get started before a depression came. Some of these men have gone through two depressions. The people who owned this land really got more than it was worth, based on its producing capacity.

Farmers' Creditors Act
But there is another side to the story. I have heard of some very pitiful cases in Ontario of farmers who had sold their land and gone to live in a village or town, having just barely enough to keep them going. The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was passed and these people found that their interest was reduced, or in some cases stopped altogether. These interest payments were all that they had to live on. The person buying the farm, even at too high a price, may be in debt, but at least he has the land to till and is able to grow some potatoes and get some meat and vegetables which the man who sold the farm cannot get.
Although I have not the full details before me at the moment of the many cases with which I am familiar, I do know of one man living in my own village of Flesherton who is blind and who has had the most slashing reductions made in his interest payments for the last two years. I cannot defend a thing like that; from the human point of view it is indefensible. The man on the land at least has a chance of getting some milk and cream and meat and vegetables, but the man who formerly owned the property has not this opportunity. This particular case may touch our hearts more because of the affliction of the creditor, but there are many others just as deserving. I know of women living in the villages throughout Ontario who are worrying themselves to death because the small incomes which they had have been halved or at least very much reduced.
There is another aspect of this problem in Ontario. Any one who has money to-day is afraid to lend it to a farmer. Therefore, our young skilled farmers, the very people we want to keep on the land and really the only people worth keeping on the land from a production point of view, cannot get loans to enable them to buy farms.

They try to manage, or their fathers may try to help them, but anyone who knows anything of farming to-day knows that it is impossible for a man to make enough off the land to extend his holdings to any great extent. Some of these men have a great deal of ability and energy, but they are finally forced off the farms into the cities or towns. They may not be actually unemployed, they seldom are, but if they are working they are displacing someone else. I can name scores of such cases, as can every member of this house.
Somewhere in the line someone is displaced from a job and goes on relief. Then in a
city like Toronto or Winnipeg, or maybe in Ottawa, some person thinks up a scheme of putting that fellow, who knows nothing about farming and never will, back on the land. He never gets a chance as he is not taken and put on land in Ontario and Quebec in a neighbourhood where there are schools or churches or neighbours, but put up in a part of the country where a goat could not live; yet he is expected to make a living there. We pay any amount of money to take him off relief schemes in the cities; we put him up in the north, and then after a while we pay more money to bring him back to the city, when what we ought to be doing-and I feel that this does come under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act-is to provide loans at reasonable rates of interest, amortized over a long period, to young skilled farmers. Possibly the greatest injury that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act has done-and I as one individual acknowledge some responsibility for it-is to make it impossible for the farmer who has capabilities to get a loan to enable him to start farming.

I believe that the best type of farmer-and again I am speaking only for Ontario-has made a great effort, although deeply in debt, to keep away from the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Many of them have not been able to do so, but the best have tried very hard; for they fear the thing we all fear, the scorn of the neighbours. After all, what we all want most is to be respected by those with whom we associate. So that some who deserve help most have never come under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, because they dread the stigma of it, while some who have come under it-I speak from personal experience-are hopeless from any point of view; you might save them now but you would have to do it again in five or ten years or at some time.
This does not apply to Saskatchewan-the two cases are so different. In one province the mortgages are held outside, there have been crop failures, but almost all loans in my part of Ontario are held locally and the hurt is felt locally. Had we thought when

we passed this measure of some way of lending money to the debtor so that he could pay part of what he owed, I think that would have helped.

No "information" will settle the cases I have in mind. We have made applications and have not got loans.
The other thing that the Farmers'Creditors Arrangement Act has done is to lower land values. Farm values have fallen through that and the liquidating of loans by the Ontario government, because undoubtedly they are glad to get rid of the land and are selling it at very low prices, and in cases where farmers have to retire through ill health or other compelling circumstances they must get rid of their farms. I find in my own immediate neighbourhood that a good many farmers have gotten old age pensions and turned their property over to the government as a last resort. They had to do something and that

was the thing they finally did; they signed their property over to the provincial government and took twenty dollars a month. In many cases-I can think of three at the moment-the man being the older got the old age pension, but he has since died, and I do not know what is going to result from a condition of that kind, w'here the woman on the farm cannot get a pension and does not own the farm. All of this is indirectly linked with the lowering of farm' values through our very peculiar handling of the matter. I urge in the wrong place, and will in the right one when I get another opportunity, that instead of a "back to the land" we evolve a "stay on the land" policy so that young men will be encouraged to remain on the farms when they want to stay, as many of them do, rather than shove them off and spend great sums of money to get unsuitable people on unsuitable farms.

speechtext: I have just one short suggestion to make to the minister, in connection with amendments co this act. It is contended that section 142, subsection 2, along with section 143, subsection (j) must be interpreted in such a way that a farmer who once has had a proposal approved is not able to make an assignment under the Bankruptcy Act. The contention is made in that regard that, in all these cases where a farmer has not been able to live up to the proposal-and in many cases that is so, particularly in the drought area of the west-he is refused a discharge under the provision? of bankruptcy proceedings because he has committed an offence under the Bankruptcy Act. The courts have no jurisdiction to grant a discharge, whatever may be the cause, if the farmer has ever made a proposal for a composition which has been acted on. I merely wish to direct these particular sections to the minister's attention so that when the bill is before the house he may have had an opportunity to consider the contention that is made.

maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT

speechtext:
I gathered from an
interjection which the Minister of Finance made when the hon. member for Weybum was speaking that he was under the impression that the board of review had adjusted debts in some cases-I understood him to say, in thousands of cases-where there was no privity of contract. The boards of review in Saskatchewan have never undertaken to adjust debts in those cases; for example, where somebody bought a piece of land subject to a mortgage to which he was not a party and later applied for the adjustment of that debt the boards of review in Saskatchewan-both the old board

Farmers' Creditors Act
and the new one-have refused to interfere because, they said, there was no privity of contract. I suggest that the minister give consideration to a provision making available the benefit of this amendment to the act to those who in the past have appeared before those boards and received no consideration. I know of several cases where, because of the fact that the only debt was the debt owing on the farm and the person who was on the farm had not made the original mortgage and was not a party to it, the board refused to formulate any proposal. Under the law as it stands a man cannot, as I understand, make a second application, so that those people who have in this regard been refused any help under the act will not get any unless there is provision for the making of a second application.
There are other cases where the board would have made a proposal dealing with the debts where there was privity of contract, but the main debt was of this nature and so they said they could not make an effective proposal at all. Now we are making this change, I submit everybody should be permitted to have the benefit of it. That is just as important, I think, as giving the right .to people whose cases were dealt with in the past by the first board of review to have their proposals reviewed, which I think should also be done. For example, when an order is made by the present board of review, there is a crop failure clause under which, upon the production of a certificate from the sheriff of the district that there has been a crop failure in the area where the farmer's land lies, all payments are postponed automatically for one year. That may not be the exact wording of the clause, but that is, I believe, its effect.
Again, there are cases where there has been a great change in the farmer's circumstances from the time the first order was made. I do not suggest that there should be provision for a second application as of right, but I do suggest that there should be some machinery whereby, if just cause can be shown, an order can be made by some competent judicial official that the applicant may apply for further consideration of his case, by the board of review, so that he may get the benefit of these amendments and also in proper cases a review of a proposal made by the first board of review.
Before I sit down I should like very much to congratulate the minister and the government upon bringing down these amendments, and particularly the one providing for discontinuance of the provisions of this act in certain provinces. Since the beginning of this parliament I had heard a great amount of dissatisfaction expressed from other provinces in regard to this act and I was afraid that so much pressure would be brought to bear that the government might consider repealing the whole act. I think everyone from Saskatchewan will agree with me that the act has been and still is fulfilling a need in that province that simply had to be and still has to be met, and so I think everybody is satisfied that the act should continue to be in force in Saskatchewan for some time to come. I believe even the creditors are satisfied with the administration of the act in Saskatchewan because the apparent large reduction of debt is a reduction more or less only in form. The board of review has cut the debts down only to the amount that they figured the farmer was able to pay, and they certainly have left it at that amount. Every fair-minded creditor, after he has come out from a hearing by the board of review, realizes that the board has left him all that he could hope to collect anyway. The fair-minded creditor realizes that there has been a fair writing down of the debts of the farmer to an amount that he can handle, and that there has been no real hardship to anybody. So I say that there has been a great deal of satisfaction, especially in connection with the administration of the act in Saskatchewan under the present board of review, and when the time comes to appoint further boards, as I suppose will be done in order to cope with the work, I hope the new board will be at any rate under the general supervision of the present chairman of the present board of review.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, possibly I am looking through the glasses of a retail distributor when I make some criticism of the administration of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in the province of Manitoba. I have always thought the act was very unfair. I have regarded it as cheap legislation, although I have always felt that the good farmers of this country have every right to protection at a time when they find it very difficult, from causes for which they are not to blame, to pay their debts. I call it cheap legislation for this reason, that if the government wants to do something for the farmer, why not do it at the expense of the country as a whole? Why put the entire load on the unsecured creditor, and particularly on the retail merchants? The farmers of this country were entitled to protection; there is no doubt about that, and I agree with what the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) said in her discussion of the act. But this is no time to make valuations of a farmer's assets upon which to base the debt which it is calculated he will have to
Farmers' Creditors Act

pay in the future. Land has no value to-day compared with what it had in the days when the debt was incurred. In 1929, when the depression set in, nobody knew how long it was going to last. Many farmers found that they needed credit, and they could not get it from the banks or the loan companies. Right here I want to make this statement, that I believe the banks and the loan companies have forfeited every right they ever had to do business in this country at any time, now or in the future.

maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext: Close them all out.

maintopic: FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Certainly.
Why did they lose faith in this country? I venture to say that when times are good again and land values high, they will want to be doing business again. I have been in the loan business for a long time, and I have known these loan companies to refuse to accept payment of loans without a three months' bonus, but they would gladly do it to-day. They missed their chance, and because they missed their chance, has the government the right to say that they shall get their money, or that the unsecured creditors of this country are the men who will take the loss?
I know as many farmers who are suffering from the injustice of this act as I do retail merchants, and I should like to cite a case or two.
A man sold his farm-at a high price, I admit. The farmer had been farming for many years, but he sold the farm and moved into town. A number of years went by, from 1929 to 1933. but he got no revenue from his farm. He was lucky to have a bank account to support him. After some years he wanted the farm back, and in the meantime the man who had bought it had never paid a dollar of principal on the mortgage on the farm. All the farmer wanted to do was to get his farm back, but he could not do so.
Another man sold his farm for $10,000 cash, and immediately bought another from his neighbour at half the price, paying no cash but taking over a mortgage of $5,000. He then proceeded to gamble away every cent of the $10,000. Five years went by and the mortgagee never got a cent from that farm. Finally, it was to be sold for taxes. The original owner at a hearing of a board of review offered the man $2,000 to get off the farm, but the board would not agree to it.
What time is this to make valuations and say that a man's debts shall be adjusted

according to the value of his land and other assets? I say it is not the proper time.
I can cite another case where the board made an adjustment by which the debtor was not to pay one single cent during 1937 except the share of crop to the landlord, and for seed from the municipality. Unsecured creditors were not to get any money until 1938. This man sold three carloads of grain and bought practically a new car for which he paid about $600 in cash. The unsecured creditors got nothing, and their accounts were reduced ninety per cent in some cases.
Many an honest farmer has loaned a farmer across the road $500 or more and given him seed wheat, and now he finds that these debts have been cancelled. The banks and the loan companies, as soon as they saw a depression was on, took chattel mortgages and every other form of security it was possible to get from the farmer. No wonder the young farmers are finding it difficult to-day to get credit. In view of the way this act has been administered, I can see no reason why anybody should extend credit.
Again I say that the loan companies and the banks, in our province at least, have lost the right, if they ever had any, to do business, and I hope they will not get the opportunity again. I say this as representing a farming constituency. I have every sympathy with the man who wants to pay his debts. There should have been a debt adjustment; there is no doubt about that, but like the hon. member for Grey-Bruce, I say the best men, the honest ones, are not the ones who are taking advantage of the act. I think the act will have to be continued, but let us have some justice in its administration. Why should the retail merchants and the unsecured creditors be the ones to help keep the farmer on the land? Let the whole nation do it; because when prosperity returns to the farmer the whole nation will benefit. The unsecured creditors will have to take a loss, and it will just be a memory. I figure that the act was a vote-catcher right from the start, and was not properly administered. I am sorry some criticism is due the government, as this is the third session of this parliament and it is the first time the act has been amended. I hope it will be made more workable, particularly in Manitoba.

with the hon. member for Grey-Rruce (Miss Macphail). I agree wholeheartedly with the last speaker (Mr. McDonald, Souris). If ever there was an act passed by any government to destroy the credit of the farmer, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was that one. If I had been in the house when this act was passed I would have voted for it. I do not advocate its cancellation, but one thing I do advocate is a change in the administration of it, because very unfair judgments have been rendered in certain cases. I will quote one example. A farmer in Carleton county had a large mortgage on his farm. He had to borrow $500 from an old couple in the village who had retired. He borrowed another $300 on a note from another farmer who could ill afford to lend him the money but who did so to enable him to pay a hospital bill. Then this farmer applied for an adjustment of his debts. It came up before the judge, and what did the
judge do?-He reduced the mortgage by half,_
with which I agree-but he cancelled the $500 note and the $300 note. I claim that was an injustice; it should never have been done. It is the administration of the act which is at fault. When this act was passed it is true the farmers were in hard straits. I agreed with it at that time.
The hon. member who spoke last said this act was passed to get votes. If my memory is correct practically all the members in the house at that time supported the act. But when it is said that it was an act passed to secure votes, I am afraid that during this past year it was used to secure votes. A farmer, the president of the Liberal association in Carleton county, applied for an adjustment of his debts under this act, and he got a most favourable adjustment. Then what did we find this farmer doing? Going out to every farmer in the county of Carleton and saying: "If you vote for Mr. Hepburn I will see that you get the same adjustment as I got." Now, that is politics.
I think that was boasting.
How did it work?
It did not work out in Carleton county.

headed by Mr. Justice Hope, would be affected by political considerations in making any award. I say that in all seriousness because I do not believe my hon. friend intends that, but that is the impression his words would convey.
It was the judgment of Hon. Mr. Justice Hope that I was referring to a moment ago in connection with the cancellation of those notes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, that is different from a political criticism.

I venture to say that if any farmer who desired a favourable adjustment of his debts approached any justice in Canada he would certainly not get anywhere with him; it would not have any influence on his decision.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No charge of political interference has ever come to my attention with respect to the adjudication of any board of review. I am bound to say that in fairness to all of them.

I agree with that, but the last speaker said this act was passed to secure votes, and I am saying that the president of the Liberal association of Carleton county told farmers that if they voted for Mr. Hepburn he would help them to get a favourable adjustment of their debts. Therefore I think there is as much politics with the present government, if there is any at the present time, as when the act was passed. And I know there is none.
I would like to see a change in the administration of this act. I would not like to see the act cancelled, but I am afraid that if it continues in force and we get decisions of the kind that have been given in some cases in the past we are going to ruin the credit of the farmers. I say in all sincerity that any farmer in the county of Carleton who has had an adjustment of his debts has destroyed his credit in any store or bank or anywhere else in the country. I have had experience with it through adjustments under this act and I have never' said a word. I have had my own debts cancelled-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh no, no.
I have had accounts owing to me by farmers cancelled up to the extent of thousands of dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is better.
I have never complained of that.

You have an indemnity.
Farmers' Creditors Act

Well, possibly that is the reason. I feel that if the government want to do something for the farmers of Canada-I have suggested this before, and the time is coming when they are going to have to do it-let them cancel all farm loan mortgages held by the government; cancel every one of them.
Santa Claus.

No Santa Claus about it. The amount of money that was spent in the last by-election in Quebec, down in St. Henry, would cancel all the farm loan mortgages in that province, and that was just to fill up a hole down there. That is the only criticism I have to offer about the administration of the act; I maintain that it is destroying the credit of the farmers.

I should like to ask the minister a question. In view of the statements made by the hon. member for Rosthern, where an application was rejected by the board of review because the person did not qualify under the act as it now stands, and where amendments may be made to the act under which that person would qualify, would he then become eligible or would he not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would have answered the hon. member for Rosthern on that point if I could have done so. As, however, I indicated at the outset of my remarks to-day, I came prepared to give a certain amount of information on the act generally, but I rather expected, in deference to the wishes of a number of members who are not here, the kind of discussion that has occurred to-day to take place either on the second reading or in committee of the whole on the bill itself. Therefore I have not sufficient knowledge as to what the legal consequences of an amendment such as is now contemplated would be with respect to those who could not qualify prior to it. However, I shall give consideration to all the points which have been raised in this discussion and be ready, I hope, not to deal with everything which may be put forward but to give such information as is possible on the second reading or, more particularly, and perhaps more suitably, in committee of the whole on the bill itself.
I am more than gratified in connection with this thorny subject to find the very pleasant welcome which my efforts to deal at least partly with the situation have received at the hands of the committee. I expected quite a difficult time; I still expect it. I do not remember, in the course of a rather long administrative career, having had a more difficult piece of legislation to apply to the
(Miss Macphail.]
widely varied conditions of Canada than this Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Every member has spoken out of bis knowledge of the circumstances affecting the people with whom he is individually familiar in his own district or his own province, and I am quite sure that every member in so speaking has done so with all sincerity and in all good faith. But to attempt to create a machine which will deal with all those varied conditions, or to attempt, as some members would, to set up conditions so that a board of review would have to do this in such and such a case or would have to do that in the other case, would be a very great tasK. You run immediately into the fact that conditions elsewhere demand different standards, and therefore you must have discretion on the part of your judicial body. The moment you commence to build regulatory fences around your judicial body, that in these circumstances you must do this and under those circumstances you must do the other, you run up against the tremendous variety of conditions existing from one end of this country to the other, and you cannot set up regulation which would be nationwide in its efficiency and scope.
All that you can do, Mr. Chairman, beyond what is now contained in the act, is to see first that there is a judge of the high court, which is one of the best guarantees of impartially from every point of view. When I say that, it does not mean that judges are perfect, but it is the best we can do, and then we must see to it that we associate with them men of high character in the capacity of debtors' representatives on the one hand and creditors' representatives on the other. From my experience, the more you surround that body with regulations the more difficult you make it for them to work out a solution for the individual farmer under the widely differing circumstances of agriculture from the rocky coast of Nova Scotia to Vancouver Island in the west.
Broadly, I am very well pleased with the reception that has been given the honest proposals, and of course I shall have to consider, when the bill reaches the committee, such other concrete suggestions as may be made for further amendments. The discussion this afternoon probably will give me an opportunity to present more information when the committee stage is reached. Possibly hon. members might now allow the resolution to pass and the bill to be introduced, so that they might study the matter we are talking about, thus making it a little easier to discuss it at the next stage.

Farmers' Creditors Act

There is just one suggestion I want to make to the minister before we pass this resolution. I fully appreciate the position of the hon. member for Souris when he says that in his district the unsecured creditor receives no consideration whatever and that the secured creditor is the only one who receives consideration before the board of review. We have had two boards of review in Saskatchewan. Under one of these boards our situation was much the same as that mentioned by the hon. member for Souris. The secured creditor received every consideration; the unsecured creditor received none. At the present time we have a board of review that gives consideration not only to the secured creditor but to the unsecured creditor, and we find that the board is working very, very much more satisfactorily than it did before.
I am afraid, when the minister says he is going to set up two boards of review, that we may have one board giving one kind of decision and the other board giving the othei kind of decision, and there will be no uniformity at all. I would ask the minister to consider the advisability, instead of setting up two boards of review, of making the present board very much larger, with six, seven or eight members, so that it may be divided up. with three men going to one place and three to another. The chief justice, or the man who is in charge, could look over all the decisions so that we would have some uniformity in the decisions given in each province, or at least in that of Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With regard to the question raised by the hon. member I have before me, of course in great detail, the percentage reductions made by the boards of review in each province with respect to both secured and unsecured creditors. I know the hon. member for Wood Mountain will forgive me when I say that the figures do not quite bear out the full extent of his statements with regard to the relationship of the boards of review in Saskatchewan to the secured and unsecured creditors respectively. That is to say, there is an element of truth in what he says, but he has stated it rather more extremely than the figures would appear to justify.
With regard to the suggestion of the hon. member as to one board of review being divided into two, I must confess that I have given a great deal of consideration to that possibility. It would be quite beyond the physical capacity of one chairman to do what the hon. member suggests, virtually to act as chairman of two boards of review. I am assured by a number of chairmen of boards
that the work is very taxing indeed. I appreciate the problem of getting uniformity of method as between boards. In the last two years, however, we have made considerable progress towards getting uniformity of methods as between the board of one province and the board of the neighbouring province, and surely, having succeeded thus far, we shall be able to get a reasonable degree of uniformity as between two boards in the same province when we appoint them. However, we shall discuss that point again.
I should like to come back to the remarks of the hon. member for Grey-Brace. I have had time to ask a question as to just what the farm loan board did in Ontario in 1937, and I find that 515 individual farm loans were disbursed in that year to an amount of $1,033,000. That is not many, but it is 515.
In my constituency alone 515 need loans.
How many applications were made, as a result of which 515 loans were advanced?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I sent out hurriedly to get the information over the telephone.

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to prolong the discussion, but may I say that generally speaking the board, operating under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, has performed a distinct and definite service to the farmers in Saskatchewan. I would approve of extending the number so that there would be two boards of review; even the suggestion of the hon. member for Wood Mountain might be worthy of consideration. I believe that would facilitate the hearing of cases now awaiting consideration.
The chairman of the board of review has laid out plans, principles and policies to which he has adhered during the term of his appointment, and he hears about five cases per day. On that basis it will take several years for him to dispose of the cases already before him. We approve, too, the suggestion that the term " creditors " should be amplified and defined and, likewise, that the benefits of the act be extended to cases of deceased persons.
We would like to have it made definitely certain that those who have had hearings before the board in 1934 or 1935 and who, for one reason or another, have not been able to live up to the terms of the orders made, should still have an opportunity of again appearing before the board.
However, I had something else in mind when I rose to speak. Residents of towns, cities and villages in Saskatchewan are dependent upon the prosperity of rural Saskatchewan. In

Farmers' Creditors Act

fact, their livelihood depends upon the rural area. Where, as has been the experience of Saskatchewan, a great part of the province is adversely affected by drought, and where thousands of farmers find themselves unable to pay, residents in the cities, towns and villages have been the losers. This situation was recognized in Saskatchewan by a resolution passed by the Saskatchewan Legislative Assembly in 1937. The matter was made the subject of a petition in Regina. Some 13,000 individuals attached their signatures to the petition, and many others in urban centres have expressed themselves as being in accord with the suggestion that the principles of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act be extended to residents of cities, towns and villages.
There are many workmen, olerks and professional men of one kind or another who prior to 1930 invested in homes, but who to-day find themselves in such a position that they may lose those homes. The act does not apply to those thousands of people. It may well be said that in their cases voluntary adjustments would be the remedy or, in the alternative, that there should be bankruptcy. It is true that the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act are open to those individuals, but no trust company or trustee in bankruptcy will accept an estate which consists of a piece of property covered by a mortgage and subject to taxes.
In many urban centres taxing authorities have large claims against such properties, and many individuals know that they can hope for nothing in the future. They are about to lose their homes, either through the action of vendors under agreements for sale, or through the city taxing authorities, or through the mortgagee under the mortgage. This is a very real fear in the hearts and minds of many thousands of honest citizens who would pay if they possibly could, but who, under present circumstances and conditions, are losing heart. They find that the rate of interest continues at the rate which prevailed prior to 1928. I had an instance brought to my attention a few days ago with respect to a house purchased in 1928 for $7,500. Already $7,600 had been paid on it; the balance still owing on the property was $3,500, and the kind-hearted vendor under the agreement for sale offered to reduce the rate of interest from eight to six per cent. He was willing to do that only within the last few months. That experience could be multiplied in hundreds of instances.
I would ask the minister seriously to consider the absolute necessity, in so far as thousands of people are concerned-and I

shall speak only for Saskatchewan-of extending the principle of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act to those men and women, in order that they may be assisted in saving their homes.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Dunning thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 25, to amend the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Would it be possible as a matter of administration to ensure that the medical pension authorities shall have the unrestricted right to secure the authorization of medical treatment when a pensioner requires it? As I understand it, the procedure now is that with a man on pension and requiring treatment, either for the disability for which he is pensioned or for a disability which has a bearing on his general health, the pension medical authority has no right to authorize treatment, it being necessary to refer the matter to the treatment branch of the department, and the man may or may not get treatment. I submit it would be a distinct advantage and probably remove any possible conflict between the two authorities if the medical men of the commission could of their own right indicate that a pensioner must have treatment. This is applicable especially to the neurological cases. The situation is far from being a happy one as a great deal of dissatisfaction exists with regard to treatment of neurological cases. Subsection 2 of section 28 of the act reads:
When in the opinion of a medical neurological expert an applicant for pension or a pensioner has a disability which is purely functional or hysterical no pension shall be paid, but such member of the forces shall immediately be referred to a neurological centre for treatment.
I am advised that in a number of cases the treatment branch has refused to give the medical attention advocated by the pension medical authority. It may be a case where the pensioner comes under class 2 and would not receive pay and allowances, receiving simply comforts while an inmate of an institution. I should like the minister to do whatever is possible to clear up this point. The same thing might be said about dental treatment.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
If a man is on class 2 treatment, as my hon. friend knows, he would continue to receive his pension and his family would receive relief if necessary. I understand the first part of my hon. friend's question was directed to whether or not the pension medical authorities had the right to order treatment. They have the right to order treatment for observation and they do so. In so far as I am aware, there has been no conflict between the two branches. My hon. friend quoted the section of the act which confers certain power on the pensions 51952-38J
authorities with respect to neurological patients. I believe the terms of that section are carried out. I understand my hon. friend's complaint is that they do not receive pensions, not that they do not receive treatment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: My information is that they do not always receive treatment; that that matter lies entirely in the discretion of the treatment branch. I am told that the medical officers of the department are not always in accord with the judgment of the pensions medical authorities and that sometimes treatment is not secured as indicated.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: As far as I am aware, if treatment is required they get it. I do not know of any conflict such as my hon. friend mentions, although there may be some. He has stated that pensions were not allowed to certain neurological cases. He was a member of the committee of 1936 which requested that a board be set up to inquire into these cases and into the treatment of neurasthenic cases generally. That board was set up and, as my hon. friend knows, some kind of report was made. The report was tabled last year; I do not have it with me at the moment, but I can very easily get it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
My point is that if the pensions medical authorities in their judgment considered treatment to be necessary and so recommended, that authority should be final without any question by the treatment branch. The pensioner should be taken into an institution and given all necessary treatment, quite apart from observation. I feel that if the minister and the officers of the department investigate this matter they will find that there have been instances where treatment has not been extended to a pensioner even though the pensions medical authorities considered it advisable.
Then I referred to dental treatment. As an example, an arrested tuberculosis case might be returned to his home, possibly some distance from the institution. The pensions authorities might say that this man should have dental treatment for the maintenance of his health, so that he might secure proper nutrition to avoid relapse. When that recommendation reaches the treatment branch they may say that dental treatment can be extended only in a departmental institution. I have before me a copy of the regulations governing this matter. The man may live a long way from the institution and he is thus automatically barred from treatment. As he is a class 2 patient the department assumes no responsibility for the expenses of the journey to and from an institution. If a man resided at Powell River in British Colum-

bia, it might be more expensive for him to undertake a trip to the institution than to have the dental treatment done at home. I have no objection to discussing the whole appeal question, and if my hon. friend wants me to do so now I shall be very glad to. It is, I admit, a most interesting question.
As he knows, the appeal provisions were placed in the Pension Act largely for the protection and assistance of the soldiers. In my opinion-and I say this without any desire to offend anyone-those provisions were used by the crown to a greater extent perhaps than they should have been.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Appeals by the crown this year number, I think, about eighty. During one year, 1931 I believe, they amounted to some two thousand-perhaps that would cover 1931, 1932, 1933. That, I think, was consequent upon an abuse by counsel for the crown of their right to appeal. That is merely my own opinion; it is the opinion I had then and I still maintain it. A great many of those appeals by the crown were affirmed. Later on, under legislation in 1933, a reviewing officer was appointed and the effect of that was undoubtedly to stop -this very large number of crown appeals. The reviewing officer handles all these appeals and recommends them. Neither the crown as such nor the department nor the minister nor anyone else has anything to do with the matter; the reviewing officer is entirely independent; he decides on his own judgment which decisions of the quorum should be appealed. At the present time appeals are very few.
In 1936, knowing that the appeal system had not worked to the satisfaction of ex-soldiers generally, I made a proposal in the house which would have had the effect of abolishing the appeal court and bringing about some such system as my hon. friend now suggests, that is, to have really a court of review in the pension commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am not necessarily suggesting it; I am asking about the present position.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I might as well tell the story chronologically. I do not think I have forgotten anything. That suggestion incorporated in proposed legislation was put before
the committee, and the committee almost unanimously, at the instance of the returned soldiers themselves-I speak subject to correction, bu-t I think almost every association was opposed to the combination of the appeal court with the pension commission- reported to the house that that particular section which I had introduced into the bill was not approved by the committee.
I understand that there is still an agitation for the abolition of the appeal court. I may say that within a very short time a great deal of the work of the appeal court will have disappeared. The claims now outstanding before the appeal court are only 380, and in 1936, when I suggested that the court be abolished, there were something like 2,300 or 2,500, well over 2,000 anyway. Now they are down to about 300. We are giving consideration, although the matter has not reached the stage of getting into legislative form, to the question of what is going to happen to this court when it no longer has any appeals before it. That is being considered on the ground alone of the expenditure of public money, without any relation to the number of applications which the appeal court saw fit to grant. It may be advisable to make some provision in the near future for the day when the appeal court will no longer serve any useful purpose. Of course it must be remembered that some of these appointments are for ten years, and provision would have to be made for appointees now holding positions in the court.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I suppose it may be that claimants are realizing that it is useless to appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend is right. The system at present is: There is a first hearing; then there is further preparation and a further hearing before the commission; after that a quorum sits and sees the applicant and decides upon his case. By the time he has gone through that and not succeeded in getting entitlement he has probably come to the conclusion that it is not much use proceeding further. That may account for the small number of appeals more than anything else; I would not say definitely.

speechtext: As the minister quite correctly stated, this matter was given careful consideration by the parliamentary committee of 1936, and at that time it was hoped that some steps might be taken, as was said then, to take some of the judicial Starch out of the pension appeal court. A medical member was appointed to the court and certain amendments were made to the act, notably that requiring unanimous judgment with regard to appeals by the crown. Some improvement was noticeable, but in viewing the matter since then I would certainly advocate the abolition of the pension appeal court and, I would say to the minister, the sooner the better from every point of view, particularly that of the ex-service man. I believe if he took some such action it would receive the general support of ex-service men across Canada. The court is functioning with all the rigidity and severity of the procedure of an exchequer court, and I say that procedure is not proper or just when dealing with pension cases. My point is that the quorum is the last court before which the applicant is given a personal hearing. The case is reviewed subsequently by a court before which he does not personally appear. The quorum, dealing with the case from the evidence before it, always has in the background the possibility of their decisions being questioned by the reviewing officer, and possibly reversed by the appeal court. There is a tendency, as we say in the vernacular, to pass the buck to the pension appeal court.
I am of the opinion that approximately twenty per cent of the cases before the appeal court, and disallowed, should have received the benefit of the doubt. However, the general attitude of the quorum has been not to take any chances on their decisions being reversed. Certainly the statistics show that, so far as appellants are concerned, the appeal to the court is a joke. The severity of the procedure works to the disadvantage of the appellant. Less than one per cent of

the appeals are allowed, I am informed, although a higher percentage of appeals by the crown are allowed. I think if the minister wishes to make certain that the applicant gets the benefit of the doubt, particularly in the class of cases now under review, the earlier the appeal court is abolished the better for the appellants.
Suitable provision might be made for the retirement of members of the court and the staff, so that no hardship would result. I must point out, however, that the main consideration is that there must be more generous treatment in accordance, I believe, with the intention of parliament. I believe that more generous and sympathetic consideration must be given, certainly in connection with applications where the benefit of the doubt might be given.

speechtext: I have had several occasions to take notice of appeals made by the government against the decisions of the pension commission.
