maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Why should the government
appeal from a tribunal which it has appointed itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That happens quite frequently. The crown may appeal from a court set up by itself, such as an appeal from the exchequer court to the supreme court. In 1930, when this new machinery and set-up was established, it was considered by those of us who were working on the framing of a pension act and of creating this machinery, that unless the crown were given the same right of appeal from the decisions, there might be created in the minds of the judges or of the commissioners or of the members of the tribunal the idea that they were there to protect the crown. As a result they might not give the soldier the full benefit of the doubt to which he was entitled. Mistakes were made because the theory of the act was not clear. Prior to 1930 returned soldiers came before committees on many occasions and said that they did not want to deal with the Canadian pension commission because that commission was putting itself in the position of guardians of the treasury. Frankly, I think everybody agreed that many members of the commission probably took that attitude. In the new set-up it was decided that both sides would have a fair chance to talk. The soldier was given his lawyer at government expense and the crown had wha* was known as a commission counsel.

Supply-Pensions-Appeal Court
I	believe abuses occurred, but I pleaded only one case before a tribunal myself. At that time I challenged the commission counsel to say something against the contention which I had been upholding in order that he might not sneak behind my back and go to appeal. He allowed judgment to be given in favour of my client and three months afterwards we were before the appeal court. I told him if he had anything to say to say it then; I wanted to settle the case then and there, but he did not say a word. It may be he had received instructions he should not have received, or it may be an attempt was being made to destroy the 1930 act. Whatever it was, the fact remains that in my opinion there were far too many appeals by crown counsel.
Mr. O'NEILL: In my opinion, there is one great stumbling block in front of the returned men. When a man applies for a pension he may be confronted with the fact that when he took his discharge from the army he was medically fit, according to his statement. Possibly less than two weeks after he was discharged he found out that was not so, and may have even gone to hospital. There are also those cases of men who were in certain lines of work before they went to war but who found out on their return that they were not medically fit to carry on the same work. They were forced to take inferior positions at lower rates of pay. These men are considered as being medically fit simply because they are able to work. A man, when he went to war, may have been in a job that paid $200 a month, but on his return finds that all he can do is work at a job that pays only $125 a month. Is there any way in which cases like this could be taken care of?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
As a distinguished supporter of labour and labour causes, my hon. friend will, I think, agree that the principle laid down when this Pension Act was conceived was that a man with a disability should have that disability assessed according to his value in the ordinary labour market. That is to say, a lawyer who was earning $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000 a year before the war-there was the odd one

and was disabled, through the loss of his eyes, and prevented from carrying on his pre-war occupation, would have his pension assessed at 100 per cent on the basis of his value as a pick and shovel man in the ordinary labour market. His pension would not be computed on the basis of what he had been doing prior to the war. The people who framed this Pension Act felt that there had to be some basis upon which to work, and that is vrtiat they arrived at. Pensions
fMr. Power.]
are paid on the basis of a man's capacity to earn in the ordinary labour market. If he has lost an arm, then it is considered he is disabled to such a percentage as a pick and shovel man would be. No consideration has ever been given to a man's pre-war occupation.
Mr. O'NEILL: There is just one more observation I have to make. If that is what you pay a labouring man when he loses his value as a labourer, then a general should be paid on the same basis. When a general is awarded 100 per cent pension he should not be getting $400 a month as a pension, he ought to get $60 a month.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, February 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Neill for the second reading of Bill No. 11, respecting Japanese immigration.

maintopic: JAPANESE IMMIGRATION
subtopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE
speechtext:
I had not intended to participate in this debate, chiefly because my district of Parry Sound has no local and no immediate interest in Japanese immigration; but after listening to

Japanese Immigration
the impressive presentation of the bill by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), it was forced upon my judgment that this matter is not merely one of importance to British Columbia, but is indeed of national concern. Therefore let me say at once that I desire to discuss the subject from a national standpoint.
The district which I have the honour to represent has its own very special problems and difficulties which on this occasion it would not be proper for me to discuss. But I would not truly represent the innate loyalty and the sympathetic citizenship of my people if I did not voice to the hon. member who introduced this bill our understanding of the gravity of the situation which confronts, in this matter, his people in British Columbia. It can truly be said of provinces as of individuals that, when difficulties occur, friendship divides our sorrows and doubles our joys, and I would say to the hon. member who introduced the bill that the friendship of the district of Parry Sound towards the great province of British Columbia is, I believe, typical of the friendship of the entire province of Ontario in its sympathetic attitude towards this problem, although not many Ontario members have yet discussed the bill.
This debate has furnished, to my mind, an outstanding contribution to the tolerance, and forbearance of the different provinces of Canada and their representatives in this house, and their loyalty to the spirit of confederation at a time when, perhaps, as between provinces we may find it desirable to reinforce our loyalties. We have heard these grave issues put forward by nearly every hon. member from British Columbia, in such impressive language as to command our sympathy, but with a tolerance of expression which is a great and lasting evidence of the loyalty of the great mountain province to Canada and to the British Empire.
I	am fully in accord with the principle of this bill. I am equally impressed with our obligation to refrain from choosing this time in our history to enact an exclusion bill against Japan. The figures given yesterday to the house by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) covering Japanese immigration under the existing agreement impressed me, as they must have impressed every hon. member, with the fact that Japan has kept, yes, better than kept, the agreement which she made with us, not only in the letter but in the spirit of her agreement. Eighty-one Japanese immigrants a year entered Canada during the past five years, when pursuant to the agreement they could have sent us 150 each year. Under the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I ask, Is this
the time to pass an exclusion act against Japan, without having made any friendly approach to her to alter or revise our gentleman's agreement, without having said to her, "We find our agreement too onerous; we desire honourably to withdraw after a reasonable lapse of time?" Can you imagine the mother of parliaments, in the present plight of world affairs, taking such a course? What would be thought of us in London to-morrow were we to pass this bill to-night?
I am not one who believes that in fiscal matters, tariff matters or any other issues, we should slavishly follow the desires of the mother country unless we are assured that the interests of Canada prompt us so to do. We are growing up. We have attained a stature of power and privilege which a few years ago we did not enjoy. But therewith we have assumed an added responsibility. Remembering this, and weighing all the facts, is there any hon. member who would choose this time to pass an exclusion act against the Japanese? It has been demonstrated to my satisfaction by the Prime Minister, and beyond all doubt, that were we to pass this bill to-night, British Columbia to-morrow would be in no better position than it is under the agreement of to-day.
On the other side of the picture, what might the possible consequences be? Can we forget that if very serious consequences, consequences we hesitate to contemplate as even possible, resulted from our conduct in passing this bill, who would bear the brunt of trouble? Our courageous, loyal, much-beloved friends who live on the Pacific coast in British Columbia would undoubtedly bear the brunt if trouble ensued.

maintopic: JAPANESE IMMIGRATION
subtopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE
speechtext: We are bearing it now.

maintopic: JAPANESE IMMIGRATION
subtopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE
speechtext:
Of course my hon. friend is right. They are bearing a burden now or the members of this house would not have felt such a sympathetic desire to help that province. But will the hon. member indicate to me any of the nine provinces which since confederation have not borne to some extent a special burden in the interests of the unity of Canada and the spirit of confederation?
I have mentioned the mother of parliaments. Can we be unmindful of the history of the past two years? Can we forget that crisis after crisis have arisen in Europe, in the Mediterranean, in India, in Egypt, and lastly in the orient, as to which those British statesmen who have been at the helm during that trying period have had to show great judgment and great forbearance, forbearance which at times, with our conception of the British flag and British traditions of the past,
Japanese Immigration

we have sometimes marvelled they were able to maintain? But with all the differences that might rightfully exist as to this incident or that and the course that has been followed in the motherland with reference to it, who is prepared to say, bearing in mind the conditions of armament and preparedness or the lack of it through the years, that in the main the sacrifices and forbearance which the British statesmen have shown have not been in the interests of the British Empire, including the interests of Canada? Then, Mr. Speaker, if that be so, if that be a reflection towards which we are entitled to direct our minds in a discussion of this problem let us, as my hon. friend across the floor did the other day, give testimony to our judgment and our own forbearance in this matter, which has in one sense an international or world aspect. Most great world conflicts, Mr. Speaker, if you go back in history, have been touched off by some incident in itself entirely insignificant as compared with the results that have followed.
The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) made, in my view, an extremely helpful contribution to this debate. He has declared that in its present form he will not vote for this bill. He suggested, in a desire, I believe, to be helpful, a possible solution, to the effect that we should pass this bill with the appropriate amendments which would prevent it from coming into operation until so proclaimed by the governor in council after a period of one year or some longer period He suggested that that might meet the thought or feeling in the house that it would be dangerous to pass this bill in its present form. May I with the greatest respect for the right hon. gentleman, so far as his discussion of this problem is concerned, suggest to the house that that solution entirely overlooks the oriental attitude of mind. I do not think, if that course were followed, we could hope to mollify Japan by saying that for the next twelve months she might, under existing conditions, send 150 more of her nationals to Canada. That would not in any sense remove the sting contained in the passing of this bill.
We heard quoted by the Prime Minister yesterday an extract from a very much respected Japanese representative in 1924 with reference to the legislation which the United States was then putting into effect. What he said, in short, was: "It is not with Japan a question of expediency." Had he been discussing our bill he might have said: "It is not with Japan a question of twelve months more freedom to send 150 more of our nationals to enter Canada. No, it is a question of principle with Japan," this Japanese
[Mr. Slaght.j
representative said. "It is a question of respect for our nation; it is the injury to our national pride which would follow." As Professor McKenzie puts it-I am not quoting him exactly, but this is in effect his conclusion that was quoted yesterday-the danger in exclusion lies in the mental attitude it provokes. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we know enough of Japanese pride and of the magnificent traits of a kind which that nation has evolved, her courage and her national pride, to realize that to permit 150 more of her nationals to enter this country within the next twelve months would be a sprat indeed if we attempted, as our conduct would imply, to use it as a solace for the injury to her national pride. If that be true, I believe that this discussion has literally been a good thing for the house and for Canada. I believe that from it we emerge with a fresh sense of our responsibility in present-day times, a fresh sense of our responsibility as a nation which arises from the greater power as a nation which we have of late years acquired.
Let me conclude with this thought, directed in the main to the hon. gentleman who so ably proposed this bill, and directed also to the members representing British Columbia whose special burden, he said, this is to bear, that the sunshine is stronger than the tempest and the storm, and there is always a far horizon for onward-looking men.

Mr. Speaker, it might be asked why a member from an eastern constituency should wish to take part in this debate, but as has been so ably stated by my hon. friend the member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slagbt), this is a question which affects not only British Columbia but the whole Dominion of Canada. While at first sight it might appear that the citizens of the constituency of Stormont, which I have the honour to represent in this house, are not directly affected by the issues raised in this bill, they are from a national point of view affected, and it is from this angle that I desire to speak upon it.
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, may I associate myself with the very wise remark made in the house yesterday by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) when he said that we should be most careful in our words upon this subject, that no word should be spoken which might be construed as an affront against any other nation. With that thought I am entirely in agreement, and I believe hon. members who have spoken have followed that advice.
I had the good fortune during the course of last year to make a trip to that beautiful

Japanese Immigration
province of British Columbia. Among the many things which I saw there, among the beauties of the province, without referring to them in any more specific manner, may I simply say that the city of Victoria with its beauty, the city of Vancouver with its tremendous possibilities, are sights which have remained in my mind.
But there is another thing which has remained in my mind, and that is the oriental question. I can quite sympathize with hon. members from British Columbia, because as travellers in that province, no matter where we went, whether in the hotel, in the theatre, in the restaurant, or as we went through the farms or along the coast where we saw what was going on in the fishing industry, we were struck with the magnificence of that province. I know I express the sentiments of hon. members when I say that our sympathy goes out to the people of British Columbia in respect to these burdens which they have to endure.
Unfortunately, while to them it may appear to be a question of a local nature, it is chiefly a question of an international nature, and one linked with the policy of Canada in international affairs. The international policy of Canada has been declared to be one of strict neutrality. With that policy I am heartily in accord. Some hon. members do not agree with that policy. There are also people and groups outside the house who disagree with it and who two years ago would have liked to see us impose sanctions against Italy. There are others who would like to see us take a stand with reference to the government in Spain. There are others who would like to see us impose a boycott on Japanese merchandise coming into this country. I saw the other day in a Montreal newspaper a picture of a street scene in Montreal depicting a parade organized and engineered in favour of a boycott of Japanese merchandise. Fortunately the authorities stopped the parade, and I believe that was a good thing from an international standpoint. I believe also that the same policy of neutrality which we put into effect as far as these other countries are concerned should be considered with reference to this bill. What would be the position of this country if we adopted this bill? It has been referred to as an exclusion act so far as Japanese are concerned. If we were to adopt the bill we should be going against our policy of strict neutrality. The act would be one which might be construed as hostile to Japan, and which in present conditions which are fraught with
great danger might very well cause a great deal of trouble.
I believe that the proper solution is that suggested last evening by the Prime Minister when he spoke of conciliation and of agreements which had been entered into between this country and Japan. He referred to an agreement entered into in 1928, by which Japan undertook not to send more than 150 immigrants a year into this country. From 1929 to 1935 the average number of Japanese coming into this country was 100, and during the last five years the average was eighty-one. True, this does not take into account the number who entered from Japan surreptitiously, but it would be impossible even by the bill which is before us to-day to do away with that angle entirely. We have the assurance of the Prime Minister that various departments of the government are doing what they can to solve this difficulty.
I therefore say that I am in agreement with this bill in principle, but would suggest that this is a most inopportune time to pass it. I believe this is an inopportune time because of the seriousness of the international situation. I believe we can well look to Great Britain and the United States for an example so far as this is concerned. Neither of these countries has seen fit in the tense international situation through which we are passing to do anything which might be construed as hostile by the countries which are at war. I believe also that it would be inadvisable to have a division upon this bill at the present time. It is therefore my hope that the hon. member who presented this bill so well may now deem it wise to withdraw it.

speechtext:
It was not my intention at first to speak on this bill. However as representing the other extreme of Canada geographically I think it fitting that I should make at least a few remarks on what, it seems to me, should be the broad Canadian view. The constituency which I have the honour to represent is situated at the extreme southeast corner of Canada, farthest away from the province to which this bill is of chief concern. The subject matter and the effect of the bill briefly are the exclusion of Japanese from Canada. I find on looking through Hansard for years gone by that this is an old topic; it has come up a number of times. I think it would be advisable to look back and see the reasons why a similar law was not passed on former occasions when the matter came up for consideration.
Japanese Immigration

The last time that the Japanese question was discussed in full detail was in 1923. On that occasion the question before the house now was argued, very ably, by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). At page 1449 of Hansard for that year the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in a short sentence gave the reason why the Japanese should not be excluded at that date. In other words, in 1923 the house saw fit to refuse to pass this law. Therefore, unless conditions have changed ; unless times are different; unless there is some reason for changing that view, I submit that we should follow the policy which was agreed upon and adopted at that time. I should like to quote from Hansard for 1923, at page 1449. where the then Prime Minister said:
The Japanese government offered itself to restrict the number of persons coming into the country in accordance with arrangements which might be made between the government of Canada and the government of Japan.
This is the part I wish to emphasize:
It was a matter, I think, mostly of national pride with the Japanese. They desired to preserve, in the face of the world at all events, the right of their citizens to go anywere-
That, Mr. Speaker, seems to have been the reason why at that time we did not see fit to exclude the Japanese from coming into Canada. As the Prime Minister stated, the Japanese were willing to fix the number of their nationals who could enter Canada. An agreement was later made, under which that number was limited to 150. If that is the only price we have to pay in order to avoid hurting the pride of Japan, particularly with world conditions as they are to-day, it appears to me that we should take the broad Canadian view and realize that by sacrificing that agreement and excluding the Japanese we would be offering an affront to that nation. It appears to me that this would be an inopportune time to take the drastic step contained in this bill and change the policy which has been followed up to the present time and which it was not thought wise to change in 1923, when conditions were entirely different. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni admits that the agreement in regard to the 150 Japanese was carried out. As I remember it, the Prime Minister, in referring to this matter last night, said that the Japanese who had come in under that agreement numbered one hundred or less annually.
If we pass this bill, in effect we are going to hurt the pride of Japan by saying, "We do not want you," or "We think we are better; we think we are superior." There is nothing that a man or a nation will resent as much as something which touches his or its national pride in that way. The hon. member for Comox-

Alberni admitted in 1922 that we should not do anything which would interfere with the trade between Canada and Japan. That reference appears at page 1543 of Hansard for 1922. Perhaps the most eloquent words ever heard in the house were those used by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni in closing the debate in 1922, when he was suggesting what should be the broad Canadian view. Those words appear at page 1547 of Hansard for that year, as follows:
If this house accepts the resolution and the government enacts not only the necessary legislation indicated in the resolution but also the registration scheme I have already indicated, I believe we will to-night do a great thing for British Columbia, a great thing for Canada and a still greater thing for posterity. For I have a vision, sir, of a greater Canada, of a Canada far greater than that which our narrow vision and our limited ambitions to-day can realize.
I think if we passed this bill we would be doing just the opposite. I believe the broad Canadian view should be that we do nothing which, under existing conditions, would in any way hurt the national pride of Japan, as the Prime Minister of the day said in 1923.

Mr. Speaker, during the course of the debate on this bill it was admitted that while it directly and primarily affected British Columbia, yet there were in it implications which would affect the international policy of Canada. Therefore I thought the voice of Manitoba should be heard as well as that of British Columbia, I have taken the position that because of the implications contained in the bill any member, be he from Nova Scotia or from British Columbia, may take part in this debate without being accused of intrusion.
In his speech yesterday the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) made it abundantly clear, in explicit terms, which appear on page 567 of Hansard for yesterday, that this bill deals with a matter no longer concerning British Columbia only, but touching the life, hope, ambition and ideals of the whole Canadian people. He realized, he stated, and was fully alive to the probabilities involved in the passing of this bill and the danger that such action would be open possibly to a wrong construction and might place us in an invidious position in the eyes of the peoples of the world in our alleged endeavour to maintain neutrality. The right hon. gentleman made his position clear, as one would expect him to, and in doing so he followed the traditional British policy that where there is an issue before the house involving the safety of the realm, it must be considered without any partisan thought. The

Japanese Immigration
right hon. gentleman, speaking not only as the leader of a party but also as a citizen concerned with the welfare and safety of Canada, took that position. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) followed the same course. He has pointed out in this and many other debates, and throughout the country, that the first consideration and paramount concern in the mind of the government must be that it shall do nothing which might be a contributing factor to bringing Canada into a war.
Do hon. members realize what would be the enormity of our offence in passing this bill, which on the face of it is so innocuous and seemingly free from harm, if that action resulted in international misunderstandings and wrong interpretations? Everybody knows that parties in an international, national or personal conflict always seek the motives underlying any act which might have a bearing upon the conflict. What, I ask you, would be the reaction of Japan if we passed this bill? The hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) has made a presentation of the bill in that splendid manner we always expect from him, an expectation in which we are never disappointed. I say to him that despite all his arguments, convincing and earnest as he may be in his presentation, that which will be remembered and enlarged upon will not be his argument, but rather some words which may be taken from the context of his speech and which may have no bearing upon his argument at all. As all public men know, sometimes a single sentence is taken from the context, although that sentence may not convey the meaning of the arguments which have been adduced.
I say to the hon. member for Comox-Albemi that I am satisfied that if this bill were to pass and Japan were to deal with it, the words used by him on page 556 of Hansard of yesterday would be the words to which they would direct their attention, and upon which they would form their judgment. These are the words of the hon. member:
We will go to China and she will say: You want to trade with us, but why do you treat us so differently from the way you treat the Japanese? And what answer can we give? We shall then be in this position: Either we shall have to reinstate Chinese immigration, which is very undesirable, or under the pressure of China's population of four hundred millions and her soldiers, we shall have to put the Japanese back where I now seek to put them.
If we are going to do it under pressure from China then, why not let us do it now with all the goodwill that comes from a free will act of justice? Let us do it now rather than under pressure later.

The hon. member for Comox-Alberni says " Hear, hear." Has anyone thought for a moment about how the passage of this bill will be considered by nations engaged in war, as they are at the present time? Would it not be considered as an unfriendly act towards Japan, and a breach of that neutrality which until now we have resolutely maintained? The answer of many would be that the Japanese would be wrong in so interpreting the bill. Possibly so; but I recall in this connection what is stated in the Monthly Summary of the Deliberations of the League of Nations. The Summary deals with the conflict between China and Japan in Volume XVII, No. 9, issued in September, 1927, and directs attention particularly to the underlying causes of the dispute. At page 197, following a report of a special committee, the assembly stated:
The report analyses the official declarations in which the Chinese and Japanese governments have stated their attitude and policy since the beginning of operations, and concludes by asserting that the two countries take very different views as to the underlying grounds of the dispute, and as to the incident which led to the first outbreak of hostilities, but that the military operations carried on by Japan against China are out of all proportion to the incident that occasioned the conflict; that such action cannot possibly facilitate or promote the friendly cooperation between the two nations that Japanese statesmen have affirmed to be the aim of their policy; that it can be justified neither on the basis of existing legal instruments nor by the right of selfdefence, and that it is in contravention of Japan's obligations under the Treaty of Washington of 1922 and under the Pact of Paris.
Despite the considered opinion of the assembly and despite the fact that the whole world believes that the Pekin incident was far too trivial to cause war, the battle and conflict still continue.
Following what I have just read we find this:
In its second report, the subcommittee stated that the present situation in China was a matter of concern not only to the two states in conflict but, in a greater or less degree, to all states. Many powers were already directly affected in the lives of their nationals and in their material interests. But even more important was the interest which all states must feel in the restoration and maintenance of peace. It was the league's duty as well as its right to attempt to bring about a speedy restoration of peace in the far east, in accordance with existing obligations under the covenant

and the treaties. It could not be admitted that the conflict could of right be settled only by direct methods between the Chinese and Japanese governments. On the contrary, any appropriate means by which peace might be reestablished, in conformity with the principles of the covenant and the provisions of existing treaties, must be examined. Even at this stage of the conflict, before considering other possibilities, further efforts must be made to secure the restoration of peace by agreement. The league could not lose sight of the tact that one party was not a member of the league and had, in relation to the work of the advisory committee, expressly declined to cooperate in political matters with the league.
The assembly realized, as all of us do, that the war might ultimately affect not only the two countries concerned but, in a greater or lesser degree, all states. I say that for that reason Canada must not supply the match to light the flame.
Every hon. member in the house, I am sure, has been assailed by individuals and organizations throughout Canada pressing them to take action or to enter protest against Japan. Among those who have approached me there have been men and women whom I would call pacifists. At all events they are men and women regarding whose peaceful inclinations there could not possibly be any doubt. They do not know exactly what they want or what should be done. All they say is that something should be done immediately. I have asked and now ask all of them this question: Do you realize what you are asking me to do? Do you realize that in the mind of every hon. member there lies the fear that some day, as a representative in parliament, he might be called upon to vote on an issue which might mean war? I have said to those people that I prayed to God that the day would never come when I would have to make such a decision.
Some say: Why not apply sanctions? I recall that in recent years sanctions were very much in vogue. I was reading not long ago an article written by Mr. Beverley Baxter, a member of parliament in London, whose contributions appear regularly in Maclean's magazine. I have not a copy of the publication before me, but I can recall vividly what he said in response to a person in Alberta who had written to him. This man referred to the fact that Great Britain had received many rebuffs in the Mediterranean during the Ethiopian controversy and that, generally speaking, she was in a decadent position. Mr. Baxter replied to the correspondent by pointing out two prominent facts in connection with the application of sanctions. First, when Britain asked France if she could have the use of French ports as naval bases in the event of war between Britain and Italy, France

replied that at that time she was not satisfied that it was necessary to have a war with Italy. The other fact was that at the assembly of the league fifty-five nations had agreed to the application of sanctions; but when the sanctions were applied it was discovered that France and Britain, to their eternal credit, had lost out in trade operations with Italy, while many of the nations in the fifty-five which had agreed unanimously to apply sanctions had increased their trade, some doubling and others tripling their previous trade with Italy. The point I am trying to make is that when you shake the mailed fist as an answer to another nation's aspirations and hopes, then you invite retaliation.
We in Canada cannot afford to take any action that would affront Japan and that might be the subject of diplomatic negotiations. We should not take any action that would cause repercussions in trade in future years. It has been said that we have gone almost to the end of our patience with regard to this matter. I would point out again the patience shown by the old country statesmen in their handling of international complications. I stand sometimes in amazement at the forbearance which has been exercised by the British government, and particularly that exercised by Mr. Anthony Eden, the foreign secretary. Surely there was sufficient provocation in the methods adopted by Italy for any nation with red blood to fly to arms. Nevertheless Great Britain has stood for all this, and instead of there being conflict today in Europe, we have at least a state of neutrality.
I ask hon. members to look at the map of the world and consider the position of Australia. If it is true that Japan is seeking an outlet for her tremendous population, there is one country in the commonwealth which is more likely than any other to be subject to attack from the orient. That country is Australia. Australia is a vast continent, sparsely settled, with a climate suitable to orientals, and it is located just south of Japan and very easy of access. If Canada were to pass this bill and its implications were resented by Japan, the result might be the bringing of the British Commonwealth of Nations into the arena of possible war. We would be doing a disservice to Australia by contributing to a possible invasion of her shores.
When the people of Canada realize what war with all its horrors means, I do not think they will want their public men to take such action as may cause a breach of our relations with any other country. I do not say for one moment that British Columbia is not having trouble with the Japanese, but I do say that

I desire to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee a case in which I, along with the returned men and other citizens of Saskatoon, have been interested. It is the case of Mr. M. P. Morpurgo, deceased. This man was born in British Guiana. He came to Canada in 1912 and shortly thereafter to the city of Saskatoon. He was a man of very small stature, about five feet one or five feet two, and weighed about one hundred and twenty pounds; he was darker in complexion than, perhaps, any man in the house, but that, I trust, will not he held against him. He was in his own country a dentist, and in Saskatoon a dental mechanic. Although of very small stature he believed it was his duty to enlist, and did enlist in the year 1916. He performed no very glamorous or heroic act. He was never outside Canada; but he joined the forces, and I think everyone will admit that after he joined, his actions were directed not by himself but by his superior officers. If he did not get outside Canada, I trust again that no one will hold that against this soldier, but rather he is entitled to every consideration to which any other man who joined the army would be.
I cannot state that what caused his accident was anything very heroic. As everyone knows, as a soldier he was obliged to march, and in marching to wear the kind of boots and the kind of socks which our army supplies. He developed nothing very serious, merely a com on his foot; that is all; but owing to some treatment given by himself or someone else the corn became infected. To make a long story short, his leg also became very badly infected, and finally, after some years of rigorous treatment by skilful medical and surgical men, the man had to lose his leg and wear thereafter an artificial limb.

Supply-Pensions-Appeal Court
His case for pension came before the pension commission, and he was granted a pension. One Sunday night, coming from church, about eight-thirty o'clock-it was a rainy night and the streets were dark compared with the ordinary night-as this man was crossing the street he was knocked down, had his skull fractured, and died a few hours afterwards.
His widow applied for pension. The case was heard before the pension commission in November and December, 1934. and pension was not granted. The case was heard again on April 4. 1935, and there was a disagreement on that occasion. Of the two commissioners who heard the case, one believed that the widow was not entitled to pension, and the other commissioner believed that she was. There is a provision in the act that in case of disagreement another member of the commission shall be asked to sit in on the case. In this particular case the acting chairman of the commission was asked to come in. The acting chairman at that time was Mr Justice Taylor, of the Manitoba court of king's bench. Knowing that there had been a good deal of confusion and disagreement in the case, he reviewed it very, very carefully, and after reviewing it very, very carefully he was of the opinion that the widow was entitled to pension. So now the decision had become two to one in favour of the pension being granted to the widow.
But we have a reviewing officer, apparently, for the Department of Pensions and National Health, whose duty it is to review all these cases. Having reviewed this particular case he came to the conclusion that the evidence was not convincing enough. I take it that if we have a reviewing officer he must keep on reviewing, or there would be no use for a reviewing officer. This case was heard in March, 1936, by the president of the pension appeal court and one other member. On that occasion I was present and I must say that I was greatly impressed with the extreme formality which I saw in that room that day. This court-I hate the name of court in connection with this-did not sit on the same level as the lawyers engaged in the case; it had to have its bench somewhat elevated. The greatest formality was exercised in addressing this pension appeal court. There was one man hired by the crown, a lawyer, prosecuting the case, and another man hired by the government, defending. It seemed more like being in a court of law than anything else I know. So far as formality is concerned in our ordinary courts, that is the proper thing. I believe it is one of the things which make for that high regard which we all have for our courts, and it has contributed to the excellent record they have established. But in cases of this
kind I must say that personally I disagree with the form and set-up which I saw, and with the extreme formality in conducting the case. The case was heard in the month of May, 1936. After it was heard, there was no judgment given for some time. I sent communications on different occasions asking that a decision be rendered by this court, and I was finally told that owing to certain legislation which had been passed by this house, they thought there might be some advantage in rehearing the case by a third member of the court. This third member was added; the case apparently was reheard, and after the rehearing in the month of September, no decision was rendered until about the middle or later of the month of December. I am going to read part of the judgment which was given in that case by Mr. Richard:
This is an appeal by the crown from a majority _ decision of a quorum of the commission ruling death due to fracture of the skull attributable to service.
The evidence discloses that the late Mr. Morpurgo was pensioned for the loss of a leg which had been amputated in 1929 or 1930, above the thigh, and that he had been furnished, by the department, with an artificial limb: that on account of his artificial limb, his freedom of movement was somewhat curtailed; in fact, that sometimes his limb would stiffen or lock, in which ease he would have to stop and make adjustments in order to get the limb working properly again; that about 8.30 p.m. in the latter part of September. 1934, the deceased, while crossing a street in Saskatoon, was hit by a motor car and died the next day as a result of a fracture of the skull sustained in the collision. The driver of the car swore that he never saw the deceased prior to the car striking him. One witness testified before the coroner's inquest that the deceased looked in the direction from which the car was coming just before or as he left the curb to start across the street. Another witness said that just as he was hit, he turned and sawr the car. There is evidence that the car was travelling slowly at the time of, and just prior to, the collision. There is no evidence that it was travelling at an unreasonable rate of speed.
To hold that death, due to fracture of the skull, was attributable to service, one must necessarily find an absence of negligence on the part of the deceased and of the driver of the car, and, more important still, one must find that but for the deceased's artificial limb, the collision would not have taken place. The fact that the driver of the car did not see the deceased prior to the collision is, in itself, some evidence 9f negligence on the part of the driver, or, if not some evidence of negligence, is ground for inferring negligence on his part, as no explanation appears in the evidence to account for his failure to see the deceased prior to the car striking him.
There is no positive evidence of negligence on the part of the deceased. There is, likewise, no evidence that on the evening in question, his limb was not -working properly, or that he had at any time to stop and make any adjustment to it. In fact, there is no evidence

Supply-Pensions-Appeal Court
to establish or provide a basis upon which it may be reasonably inferred that the artificial limb contributed in any way to the collision. To hold that it did is to base the conclusion on pure conjecture. It is a matter of common knowledge that people with sound limbs are being run down every day on our streets.
In my opinion, the evidence does not establish that death due to fracture of the skull was attributable to service. I would allow this appeal.
The president of the court said:
I agree with the conclusion arrived at by my colleague, Mr. Richard, who would allow this appeal, and merely wish to add that in order to succeed in a claim for pension in respect of the death of an ex-soldier it must be established that the death was attributable to service. Section II (I) of the Pension Act reads as follows:
"In respect of military service rendered during the war,
(a) pension shall be awarded to or in respect of members of the forces who have suffered disability in accordance with the rates set out in schedule A of this act, and in respect of members of the forces who have died, in accordance with the rates set out in schedule B of this act, when the injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in disability or death in respect of which the application for pension is made was attributable to or was incurred during such military service."
In conjunction with section 11 there must also be read section 73, which is as follows: "Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which shall mean that it shall not be necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall be entitled to draw and shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences in favour of the applicant." Shortly after this court came into operation the following interpretation was put upon this latter section:
At this point I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members this interpretation, which personally I had never heard of until I found it in this document:
Proof or evidence of the fact must be of the same general nature as is required in a court of law, as, for instance, in a damage action for injuries or death. The method of proof might justifiably be more elastic but the proof must be positive and not left to mere conjecture, suspicion or surmise. It may happen that on a consideration of the whole case the evidence may preponderate as against the applicant, but while he would in that case probably fail in a court of law, it was intended by parliament (section 73) that notwithstanding the weight of evidence against him the applicant should succeed, but always provided a prima facie case at least is established or made in the first place, and if on the balance of the two a real and substantial, but not a fantastic, doubt in his favour is left in the minds of the tribunal or court.
Then he goes on to say:
Since this interpretation was given by the oou rt there have been several amendments to 
The Pension Act, as well as two parliamentary committees, and parliament, which must be presumed to have known of this interpretation, did not see fit to in any way amend either section 11 or section 73. We have stated time and time again that in order to raise a reasonable doubt, as contemplated by section 73 of The Pension Act, there must be some facts established from which such reasonable doubt can be inferred.
In the case before us we have nothing whatsoever in the way of facts from which we could infer that it was the deceased's inability to move his leg which caused the unfortunate accident, but on the contrary we could reasonably say that it was due to some negligence on the part of the motor car driver. That, however, does not assist the claim.
To my mind the whole case is one of pure surmise, guess, or conjecture, which, as above stated, cannot be regarded as proof. With regret, therefore, I would allow the appeal.
Now, what is the evidence in this case? The evidence is that this man was crossing Second avenue, our busiest thoroughfare, from the east side to the west. It was a night on which it had been raining, and was rather dark. Anyone driving in that city as I have done for the last number of years will know that on such a night as that it is very difficult even to know whether your own lights are on, and the light round about is not very bright. The driver of this motor car was going north on Second avenue; he was passed by a street car. At the south part of the intersection there is a safety island. The street car stopped, and again he passed that street car and slowed down, as he says in the evidence, which is corroborated, almost to a standstill. He started up from that point and his own evidence is that he was going at the rate of eight miles an hour. Two girls who were crossing the street at the same time and who said they are accustomed to driving cars say he was going at a speed not greater than from ten to fifteen miles an hour. He was asked whether or not he was attending to his business and looking straight ahead, and he said, "I had both hands on the wheel, I was looking straight ahead and I did not see this man." [DOT]
The evidence further is that the man left the curb on the east side of the street walking towards the west, the girls walking the other way. They met him eight feet from the curb and they say that at that point he was looking south, and that they, following his example, also looked south and saw the car some distance down the street. The man kept on and the evidence further is that when found he was lying with his head north; one man says the head was on the east rail of the east street car track. The evidence also says that this man was hit by the left fender of the car. I might say further that the evidence of many people is that he had

Supply-Pensions-Appeal Court
to walk with a swinging motion of his left leg which impeded his movements at all times. We have the further evidence of his wife that during his last month or two this leg was known to lock on different occasions.
Then, how far did he get? He was going across the street until he came to the street car track and at that point he was hit by the left side of the car. Had he been just one foot further across the street he would not have been hit by this car. The judgment which I have before me says that there is no evidence to show that he might not have been hit except for some negligence on his own part. It also presumes that the driver of the car is the man guilty of the accident. Well, the evidence is that this man in that car was driving at a very careful rate of speed, according to his own evidence eight miles an hour, and the greatest speed suggested by any witness is from ten to fifteen miles an hour; further, that he was looking in the direction in which he was travelling and had both hands on the wheel.
I call the attention of the committee to the fact that if this benefit of the doubt clause means anything at all, surely this is a case in which it should have been construed in favour of the applicant and not against him. There is not an hon. member of the house but will recognize that a man with that kind of artificial leg cannot walk as quickly as a man not so handicapped, and consequently when some danger is in front of him he simply cannot get out of the way as he could if he had two good legs. Is there any hon. member who believes that this man could not have made that extra foot if he had not been impeded by the artificial leg? I ask that in all seriousness.
Personally I did not know this man, but I have taken a great deal of trouble to inquire from our own officials in this department in our own city. They felt very keenly about it; they have made representations. I have talked to the doctors who looked after him; I have talked to many returned soldiers who knew him intimately and knew the difficulty he had in walking, and their unanimous opinion is that he would have been perfectly clear and safe but for the fact of his having an artificial leg.
A minister of the crown came to me one day and said, " What have you been saying about the president of the pension appeal court?" I said, " I don't know that I said anything very much." " Well," he said, " he came to me to say, ' Have I to stand all this abuse when I am protecting the treasury?'" That was the Minister of Finance who came to me in a very kindly spirit. He has known
me for a number of years, and he was not really trying to protect the treasury, but he thought I might have been saying something about the president of the appeal court and asked me about the circumstances. Apparently great exception was taken by the president to a letter which I had written, and which contained the alleged abuse. I propose to read this letter in order that it may be on the record. It is addressed to the president of the pension appeal court, and is as follows: Saskatoon,
December 21, 1936.
Mr. Justice Hyndman,
Pension Appeal Court,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir:
Re: #205 M. P. Morpurgo, deceased
I thank you for your letter of the 17th instant re the above case. I am very sorry indeed to learn of this decision. It is needless to say I disagree entirely with the decision. The judgment seems to be based on very fine legal technicalities. I cannot help observing that this was passed by the quorum, by a majority of two to one, one member of which was also a judge of the court of king's bench.
Persons here who are acquainted with the whole situation are unanimous that the pension should be granted. By this I mean that all those who spoke to me, and to whom I spoke, consisting of a fairly respectable number, are of this opinion.
The meaning of the legislation giving the benefit of the doubt would not appear to have very much significance. What we really require is more in the way of real justice and less in the wray of legal technicalities.
One statement you made during the discussion of the case, when I was present, deserves more than passing notice. It was that if this case were granted it would cost the country $20,000 and that was a lot of money. I respectfully suggest that that was a highly improper remark to make. Whether it would cost $20,000 or more, or less, should not have been a thought coming into the mind of one giving judicial decision on the merit of the application.
I wish to thank you for your personal courtesies for keeping me advised from time to time regarding this case.
Wishing you the compliments of the season-
That is signed by myself. I do not know whether it would be considered the gross abuse that he was referring to if he had in mind my mentioning the remark which he made in my presence when that case was being heard. To me it seemed a very improper remark to make, to say, " If I grant this pension it will cost $20,000, and that is a lot of money." I do not believe it is any part of the duty of any court to take into consideration whether a judgment will cost $20,000 or more or less, or to have anything whatever to do with the amount of money involved. That is up to the parliament of Canada; that has been settled by an act which has been placed in our statute books,

Supply-Pensions-Appeal Court
and the only thing the court should be interested in is whether or not the applicant is entitled to a pension. I have a letter also from the president of the appeal court, dated December 17:
I must apologize for not replying to your letter of December 8th before this, but for various reasons I did not get around to it.
With regard to this ease, I may say that at the time it was argued, we were all unanimously of the view that no claim for pension had been established, that is, that there was no proof, in the sense of the Pension Act, that the death of the ex-soldier was attributable to service. To say that his death occurred as a result of his inability to escape from the oncoming motor car, because of his leg condition, is a pure guess and conjecture only, and not proof in any sense of that term.
In fact, it would appear that the responsibility, prima facie at least, must rest on the driver of the car. This is the law of Saskatchewan and the motor vehicles act raises a presumption in law that the motor ear driver is liable for injuries to pedestrians, in the absence of proof that he was not negligent. Apart altogether, however, from this statutory presumption, it would appear that the motor car operator in this case was to blame, and he admitted that he never saw the deceased and did not know what he struck. It would seem most peculiar that a motorist at the locality of the accident, which was well lighted, and if he had his lights properly on, did not see the deceased. If the accident was caused by negligence on the part of the motor car operator, then it was not due to any fault or disability in the deceased himself.
I may add, for your own information, that the delay in giving judgment was with the object of endeavouring to make sure that we were not wrong in our view, and to make doubly sure if possible, we discussed the case with several judges of the highest courts in different parts of Canada, whom we happened to have the privilege of meeting in Ottawa- one of them being a very able chief justice, and there was complete unanimity that the claim could not be established.
I realize how much in need the widow is and it would have been a matter of great pleasure to be able to come to the opposite conclusion, but we are hound by the Pension Act and, as you know, unless soldiers can bring themselves within the terms of that act, it is impossible to giant a favourable award.
Again regretting very much indeed our inability to assist this widow, and wishing you the compliments of the season, believe me-
That is signed by the president. Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to make two or three observations. In the first place, this application was heard by a pension tribunal, and was refused. New evidence was adduced; the application was heard again by two commissioners, and there was disagreement. The chairman of the court, a justice of the court of king's bench in Manitoba, was called in, under the terms of the act. I believe he was an able man. He was once the leader of the Conservative party in Manitoba, and I take

it that able men are selected to lead that party; I assume that statement would be agreed to by hon. gentlemen opposite at all events. In any case I am prepared to say that a careful selection was made in the appointment of this gentleman to the bench. He gave careful consideration to this case and he was of the opinion that the pension should be granted.
Now I come to this last letter, in which I find what is to me at least an extraordinary thing. Apparently before the members of the appeal court made up their minds they went out and consulted judges of other courts, who never saw the witnesses, probably never read the evidence and only heard a review of the case as given by the president of the appeal court. I am wondering whether or not it was the judges who had no right to any say in this matter who influenced the judgment of the appeal court.
It has been said that a great deal of conjecture entered into the matter. Is it mere conjecture when a man, wearing an artificial limb, crosses a street on a night such as that, and has only a few inches left to go? If he had two good legs he could have made that last little distance, which certainly was not more than a foot. Am I to believe that the benefit of the doubt means anything whatever in this case? I want to put on record a few figures which I obtained the other day from the department, which may settle some of the questions raised by some of my hon. friends to-night:
Herewith is certain statistical information relating to the operations of the pension appeal court which was asked for this morning by Dr. A. MaeG. Young, M.P.

Supply-Pensions-Appeal Court
the calendar years 1936 and 1937. They do not include cases which were remitted for further consideration, applications for leave to reopen, and other miscellaneous references to the court. The gist of the statement is that during the two year period mentioned a total of 4.938 appeals were disposed of by the pension appeal court. Of these 118 were resolved in favour of the applicants, and 4,820 against the applicants. The number of applications resolved in favour of the applicants by courts of the Canadian Pension Commission during the two year period covered by this report was 1,266. It will be observed that the crown lodged appeals in only 114 of these cases and that of these 114 cases, 75 were resolved by the crown in favour of the applicant.
We have heard a great deal to-night about whether or not this pension appeal board was rendering service. I would say to the committee that if the decisions were given, as I believe they were in this case, on strict legal technicalities, where the soldier's widow did not receive the benefit of the doubt, this will explain why it was almost useless for an applicant to bring his case before the appeal court. I am satisfied myself, from what I have seen in the court itself, and from the records which I have seen, that the pension appeal court is not serving a useful purpose for the returned soldiers of this country.
I want to say, further, that once a pension is granted by a quorum of a commission, so far as I am concerned I believe that pensioner is entitled to get the pension, without the crown employing counsel to find some way whereby the pension may be set aside. I am definitely opposed-I have said this outside and I want to say it in this chamber where I can be heard by all-I am definitely opposed to the crown taking appeals from the decisions of the pension commission where the applicant has received a favourable decision. A soldier takes a great deal of trouble to present his evidence, and may get a favourable decision from the quorum. We then employ men to take from the soldiers that which our own appointed quorum gave to them. There is something wrong with that system. I am just as satisfied that in this particular case justice was not done as that I am standing in my place in the house.
I would rather take the opinions of those good returned men, and others in that city who knew the man well, who knew the conditions in the city on that night, and who knew the circumstances of the whole case intimately. They are unanimously of the opinion that the widow was entitled to that pension. I would rather take their verdict than a judgment of the pension appeal court. I do not believe in all the formalities which we have. Perhaps there may be some use for an appeal court, but the figures I have given
to-night would lead me to conclude that there is not very much reason why we should have an appeal court or why we should continue having one.
I do not wish to say anything unfriendly with regard to the personnel of the court. I believe that their point of view is not right. Perhaps I should not say this, but I do say it most kindly, that Mr. Justice Taylor was himself a returned soldier and a judge of the court. The president of the appeal court, a former judge of Alberta, is not a returned soldier. The same is true of Mr. Richard; he is not a returned soldier. I do not know whether those men look at the problem in quite the same light. I would not like to be unfair and to say that they do not, but I merely mention the point.
I do know this, that the judgment of those who intimately know the case in Saskatoon, and the judgment of those men in Saskatoon who have been trying to be fair, would be at least to me of more value and carry more weight than the judgment of the pension appeal court. I have often heard the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and other hon. members say that where there is a wrong there must be a remedy. I believe that in this case there is a wrong. I appeal to the minister and to the committee to find some way whereby this widow, who is in great need, will be given the pension which I believe she deserves.
Why was there all this delay from May until December? Why go to other judges to find out their opinions, if it was a clear case, where there was no doubt? I ask that in all sincerity. More than that, a skilled judge in the quorum wras of the opinion that there was a good case. There was some doubt at least in the minds of some. I say that under the act passed by parliament, which act I claim was misinterpreted by the pension appeal court, the widow did not get the benefit of the doubt.
Once more, before I sit down, I am going to ask the minister to give consideration to this case and, if there is any way possible, to see to it that justice is done and that she gets her pension.
