maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the facts as related by the hon. member are, I believe, substantially as disclosed by the file. The application received a great deal of consideration from the different bodies set up to deal with pension applications. I believe the hon. member gave all the facts, in so far as they are available, to the committee.
On November 13,	1934, the Canadian
pension commission decided that death was not related to service. On December 18, 1934,
618	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions-Appeal Court
the Canadian pension commission decided that additional evidence does not alter the former decision. On April 4, 1935, the application was heard by a quorum of the Canadian pension commission, commissioners Jones and Grajr. A disagreement resulted, Commissioner Jones finding that the accident was consequential upon the pensionable disability, and Doctor Gray finding that death was due to an accident which was in no way associated with the service disability.
On February 8, 1936, pursuant to the statutory provision with regard to a disagreement between two members of a quorum of the commission, the case was referred to a third member and was considered personally by the acting chairman of the commission, Hon. Mr. Justice Taylor, who concurred with Commissioner Jones and found that the soldier's death was attributable to his service.
On March 6, 1936, the reviewing officer did not concur in the finding of the quorum of the commission and directed that an appeal be lodged on behalf of the crown. Among other reasons the reviewing officer gave these for appealing the decision:
It is considered that the reasons given by the members of the quorum, who are of the opinion that death was attributable to service, are not convincing, are to a considerable extent based on conjecture and are not corroborated by the evidence given at the coroner's inquest.
It is further considered that, as entitlement decision in this case depends almost entirely upon a correct appreciation and interpretation of the evidence before the inquest as to the details of the accident, it is advisable that this claim should be completely considered by the pension appeal court, particularly in this respect, and before any final decision as to entitlement in respect of death is given.
On December 22, 1936, there was a judgment of the pension appeal court in which Mr. Justice Hyndman set forth his reasons and Mr. Richard also gave his reasons. I do not think the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) or any other hon. member will ask me to express an opinion as to the value of a judgment rendered by the appeal court. I cannot do that. I am not in a position to do it. I have not the facts before me, and I do not think hon. members, other than the hon. member who has just spoken, have sufficient knowledge of the facts to render any judgment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: And this is not a court of appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I was about to say that parliament has set up the machinery to decide on the merits of these cases. Parliament has divested itself of that duty, and has prohibited the minister from taking sides in matters of this kind. I regret to say that I

can make no suggestion to the hon. member as to what further procedure could be followed, any more than I can make a suggestion to him were he to ask me with respect to a non-appealable case in any of the courts of his province or in the Supreme Court of Canada.
It would appear that the appeal court carefully considered the case. There was some delay, but I should like to point out to my hon. friend that if anything that delay was of some value to the applicant. The appeal in this case was lodged in March, 1936, and came up for hearing in May of that year. It will be remembered by hon. members that at the session of 1936 legislation was enacted to the effect that when t'he crown had lodged an appeal, in order to succeed it was necessary that the judges be unanimous. This could have been of material 'assistance to the applicant because, if the appeal had been heard and decided in the month of May, when it first came before the court, that Statutory provision for the protection of applicants would not have been effective. When the case was heard the second time in September, 1936, that provision which gave a claimant a better chance than had existed previously was in existence. It would appear that the three members of the court who heard the case were unanimous in their decision against the applicant.
With respect to Mr. Justice Hyndman, I may say that he has had a long and distinguished career as a member of the supreme court of Alberta. Prior to that he was a distinguished member of the bar of that province. I have less knowledge of the legal ability of the other two members of the court, but I am convinced that all the members are conscientious men. I am sure that when they give their decision they do so to the best of their knowledge and ability and in all conscience according to the judgment which they think is the proper one in the circumstances. That is all I can say on the subject.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I was careful to say that the delay was due to certain legislation, but I also pointed out that the case was reheard in September and no judgment given until December. If there had been no doubt in their minds the decision could have been given at once. Instead of that, they sought opinions from other judges. If there bad been no doubt in their minds, they would not have done that. I must say that I was very unfavourably impressed by two things. The first was that in my presence it was stated by the president of the court of appeal that if that case was granted it would cost the country 820,000,

Supply-Pensions-Appeal Court
and that was a lot of money. I was present and I heard that. Then he went to the Minister of Finance and he said, "Am I to stand for abuse when I am protecting the treasury of this country?" I do not believe that is a proper attitude to take with regard to a matter of this kind. It so impressed me as to make me consider more carefully the number of cases which went to appeal and the number of appeals granted. I was perhaps cpn-sidering this matter more carefully than other hon. members who never have been in that court of appeal.
I want to say to the minister that if that is the attitude that prevails, the sooner we do away with the appeal court the better. This afternoon some hon. gentleman on the other side said that where there was a dispute and a returned man appealed, he might have his case reheard by other members of the same board. I am quite certain that there is far less formality and technicality before the quorum, where the witnesses appear, than there is before this appeal court. In conclusion I want to say that we must either humanize this appeal court or do away with it entirely.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Because this matter is one of such great importance I venture to make a few observations. I do not think a week goes by when I am in western Canada that I do not receive complaints regarding the adjudication of claims for pensions. I recall a case in which a widow came to see me not very long since with her papers and complained bitterly that she had been denied the right to a pension by the appeal court because the court had held that death was not attributable to service. I might have arrived at another conclusion-I think I did-but I am not going to say that the tribunal was wrong for that reason.
Anyone who is familiar with our jurisprudence knows that the books are filled with cases where one judge entertained one opinion and another, another. The courts of appeal finally settled what the law should be. I recall what is known as the Wakelin case in which an action was brought against a railway company in England for negligence because a man had been found dead on the right of way where he had been thrown by a train that had passed and struck him. Varying views were entertained between the trial court and the House of Lords, but finally they laid down the law which has been the law ever since and which has been applied by our courts, including the court of last resort, the Supreme Court of Canada. The law is this: Unless there is some evidence to indicate that the injury or death complained of is
attributable to some act of negligence, the plaintiff fails in his claim. That has been the universal declaration of law, and if it i$ open to pure conjecture as to how death occurred, the plaintiff cannot succeed. The reason is obvious.
Anyone who is an educated and professional man like the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) knows that the rule is that he who asserts must prove. When this poor unfortunate man was killed as a result of an automobile collision, it was the duty of those who claimed a pension to prove that that death resulted because of some defect in the appliance provided or for some reason connected with the appliance which he was using and which prevented him from escaping something about which no one knew anything. That is, the hazard that he faced was not known. It was only known that he was killed by being struck by an automobile and the assertion of the poor, unfortunate widow that the death of her husband was attributable to this appliance made necessary because of his service obviously could not be sustained. She could not prove, either by inference or otherwise, that the death complained of was attributable to anything connected with his service. That, I think, disposed of that side of the matter. I do not think that the local law in the province of Saskatchewan dealing with the question of the presumption of law when the injured person is struck by an automobile advances the matter any further.
But we must proceed one more step. The hon. member for Saskatoon has pointed out, very properly, that the statute contains a provision whereby the benefit of the doubt must be given to the applicant. But the kind of doubt to which the statute refers is not the doubt that I have indicated; it has no reference to that. The difficulty lies in the fact that if you substitute for the construction of a statute the sympathy of human nature and human kind, you always run into difficulties. That has been pointed out so frequently that I am not going to restate it. I wonder if there is anyone in this chamber to-night who would not desire to see that woman get a pension. That is human nature, and to its credit be it said, it is human sympathy.
But when you begin to apply principles that are laid down in a statute, those principles must be interpreted not in the light of the sympathy of the individuals who apply them or the sympathy of those who sit in the court and listen, but on principles that are settled by courts as to how a statute shall be interpreted. Interpretation is the duty of the court, and if it were otherwise what a mess
620	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions-Appeal Court
we would be in. If our sympathies were to govern our judgment, where would we be? I recall conclusions that in a very youthful day I arrived at, with respect to what I conceived to be a great miscarriage of justice, because my sympathy entirely controlled and governed my judgment. As one gets a bit older one begins to realize that the rules which govern the interpretation of a statute, the function of the judge or a court, are rules which have been created not for the purpose of destroying the operation of human sympathies but that justice may be done to all without fear, favour or affection. And what a stupendous task it is to administer justice at all. Justice is an attribute of the Godhead. Milton said, "Not just, not God." To endeavour to administer justice is one of the most difficult of all the obligations that can be placed upon mankind. I am satisfied, knowing Mr. Justice Hyndman as I have for thirty years and knowing that very few of my acquaintance are more sympathetic than he-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It is not a question of guessing at it; I know he is sympathetic. But one of the reasons that an appeal court was constituted as it was, was for the purpose of preventing what may be called the play on sympathy in determining ultimate responsibility.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Would the right hon. gentleman not say the same thing about Mr. Justice Taylor?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Yes, but Mr. Justice Taylor approaches the problem with a warmer sympathy than would be possible when you have to determine a pure question of law. I point out, what the hon. member for Saskatoon seems to overlook, that in the ultimate analysis this case became nothing more or less than a pure cold question of law. It is easy for us in this chamber to say that that never should be so. But unfortunately or fortunately, in determining the question of liability on the part of the crown to pay pensions, we have passed a statute of this parliament, and may I add that it is, so far as I know, the most generous statute in the world. Perhaps we in this country made one mistake, and that is the reason those four thousand cases are there. I heard the Minister of Pensions in England once say that although they had made mistakes they never endeavoured to cure them because they left the precedent for future cases to govern them, believing that to endeavour by legislation or otherwise to cure them would only invite in the end chaotic conditions. He went further;

he said, "We have never departed from the rule that beyond a given date we would not receive applications for pensions." Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: They did to some extent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am just coming to
that. W hy? Because the laying down of an absolute period of cut-off was thought to be the only method by which one could ensure against what one might call unfair claims being preferred to the pension boards. There were exceptions, but the exceptions were so few in number as not to operate against the application of that universal rule. Now we have seen fit to extend the time and extend the time until, in the year 1936, we are hearing claims that arose in 1915 and 1916. The minister hinted at it but he did not follow it up. For obvious reasons, in his position he could not very well do so. But the fact is this, that of those four thousand claims which were dismissed on appeals made by the applicants, I venture to say in eighty per cent no one appeared; it was an impossible claim from the start; it was a claim that in eighty per cent of the cases had been presented not once or twice but sometimes ten or fifteen times before they finally reached the decision which has been indicated. Now why was this done? Because, this being a new country and we never having had to face a situation like this, we realized that there were many weaknesses. These independent men who came back feeling all right said, "We are not going to bother about making application for pension," and so they did not do so. Many of them who are in good shape, though they have a right to make a claim for a pension, have not done so yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: We are receiving more claims on account of gunshot wounds now in comparison with the others than we ever did before.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Just think what a support of that position the observations of the minister are. He is now, twenty years after the peace, receiving claims for pensions for gunshot wounds. So far as I know ours is the only country in the world that is doing this.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is because the men did not desire to claim earlier.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is the very reason, of course, that the men, not feeling it necessary and desirable to make claims, did not do so. Now they are beginning to feel the effects and so now they are beginning to make these claims. Legislation on this matter has never been party legislation in this house.

Supply-Pensions-Appeal Court
There was a little attempt at it once, but we shall pass that by; broadly speaking, there has never been party legislation. Under these circumstances this legislation is legislation that has been arrived at by compromise and adjustment and giving a little here and taking a little there by men who are all returned men. In every case they fashioned and shaped existing legislation. I think it is correct-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Substantially.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: -to say that the shaping of the legislation has been done by returned men on both sides of politics.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: But the final adjudication was by men of whom two out of three are not returned men.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The final adjudication.
But it has been a question of the determination of liability by the application of principles of law. I think that is a fair
statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
At one time, I believe, the
appeal court did decide in many cases question of fact.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That was in the very
early days.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The intention I had at the
time the law was passed was that the appeal board should decide only on questions of law, and not fact; but they went beyond that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is true, because it
will be remembered one member of the quorum decided that if a man had been in France he was entitled to a pension, and this made it a little difficult for the appellate tribunal when it had to deal with the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I do not think that was
quite the decision. Perhaps the right hon. gentleman has not stated the fact quite correctly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I recollect that case
where he said, "Were you in France? Well, you will get a pension."

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That was not given, though, as one of the reasons for his decision in awarding the pension.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That is about the only
reason he ever did give, I am bound to say, which is unfortunate.
I want to get back to one thing. The hon. member for Saskatoon has said that two out of three men who decided this case were not
returned men; they were both lawyers, one a judge of fifteen or sixteen years in the appellate division of the supreme court of Alberta, and partly in the trial division, the other a practising member of the bar of New Brunswick for many years, and the third was a returned soldier and a member of the legal profession residing in this city.
One reason why that appeal court was constituted at it was, was just as the minister has said. It was originally intended they should deal with questions of law; they did have at times to deal with questions of fact as well. But in this case it is purely a question of law, and the question of doubt which has been mentioned does not arise at all, for the reasons given by Mr. Justice Hyndman in his judgment. If, for instance, there had been evidence that there was negligence on the part of the unfortunate deceased, and on the part also of the driver of the car, then the benefit of the doubt would have to go to the man; but when there is no evidence one way or the other, nothing except the bare fact that the man lies dead with a cracked skull, that does not create any presumption one way or the other. There is not even a prima facie case; there is no bent of testimony to prove anything connected with the man's death. He is dead. He was struck by a motor car. Whether that was an act arising from his own negligence or from the negligence of the driver of the car, or purely from some circumstance as to which there is no evidence at all, you have no question there upon which the application of that principle of the benefit of the doubt is to apply. It is like the case of a man who is found lying dead on the side of the right of way, and a train was known to have passed by. You could not say there was any relation between the death of that man and the passing of that train. That is what the House of Lords has decided, and the judges in the appellate division were bound by that principle of law in the absence of any proof-just keep in mind that fact- as to how the death occurred. There is no presumption one way or the other, and there being no presumption and no evidence, then of course it followed that you could not predicate liability without presumption or some form of evidence. But had there been the slightest evidence upon which a conflict arose, then it was the duty of the court, as pointed out in the interpretation placed by Mr. Justice Hyndman upon that provision, to give the benefit of the doubt to the applicant.
The minister will recall how vigorously that was threshed out in this house. The late

Supply-Pensions-Appeal Court
Doctor McGibbon was here for hours dealing with that. That was why the committee made its report. It was a difficult clause to draw, to fit into legislation; but it was done, and it merely means that if you have some conflict, however small it may be, however slight it may be, then you have liability predicated, because the benefit of the doubt must go to the applicant.
Just one step more and I have concluded, and I would not take up the time of this committee were it not for the fact that I receive many cases of this kind. I have had to tell unfortunate applicants just what I am saying now, although much more briefly, and I dare say this committee wishes it were an applicant at the moment instead of having to listen as it is doing now.
The president of the court was frank enough to say to the member for Saskatoon that they had consulted leading jurists of the country, judges. Well, I can tell him that that is a very ordinary course for judges to take who are dealing with problems not of this kind at all, but with such questions as the legal effect of a man being found dead with a fractured skull. When they are dealing with the question of legal liability predicated upon the fact that a man had been killed, they might well consult leading jurists and others, the same as doctors sometimes consult together. In fact, I remember a most eminent physician who told me that he had met one of his fellow-craftsmen, who was a surgeon from another country, and that he had discussed with him very carefully a particular case. Even doctors do that without in any sense interfering with the soundness of their own judgment or the honesty of their convictions. And the fact that judges do it is well known everywhere. When they meet together one judge will say to another: "Is there any question that the mere finding of the body of a man who has been killed in an accident by coming into collision with a motor car does not, in the absence of some proof, constitute any cause of action?" In the same way a learned physician meeting another physician might ask him whether or not he could say with certainty that the use of the most important pharmaceutical discovery of 1937 would not have injurious effects upon a man's mind, to say nothing of his life. When you have new things, and even old things, physicians have been known to talk about them to one another. So the hon. member for Saskatoon cannot predicate any great argument upon that.
I am surprised to find that we have what we may call hearsay evidence introduced into this chamber. It is alleged that the president

of the court spoke to the Minister of Finance, who told the minister, who told the house-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Do I come into this?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Oh yes, the Minister of
Finance is in this. He is supposed to have been approached by the president of the court, who asked him whether or not he was to listen to these attacks against him, because it was being alleged that he was trying to protect the treasury. But, knowing Mr. Justice Hynd-man as I do, I do not think that is exactly the way in which he would put it. I do not think it is quite consonant with our ideas of propriety that any member of the house should predicate a grievance upon a statement that somebody told him that somebody had told him that the president of the court had said so and so. That is perhaps not quite what would be expected in this chamber; I will merely leave it at that.
I am interested, as I feel every hon. member must be interested, because I frequently receive cases of this kind. I had to tell a poor lady not long ago: Unfortunately here is the unanimous determination of the court, and I know of nothing I can do for you unless you have new evidence. Once you have new evidence, you can present your case to the court once more for the purpose of having the court say whether such new evidence is of such a kind as warrants a rehearing of the case. Inasmuch as we are all interested, and inasmuch as I still believe the appeal court has served a useful purpose, not only for the state as such but for the returned men themselves, I can readily understand how human sympathy has been aroused in cases like this.
I would think less of the citizenship of Saskatoon if I were told that it did not sympathize with the widow. It is human nature that this should be so, and it is very much to the credit of human nature that such sympathies do prevail. But that has not been the method which has been used in any country I know of for the purpose of determining how these matters should be dealt with, except one. After the great civil war it was left open to any member of congress to propose that a pension should be paid to John Smith, and if he could by sufficient appeal to the sympathies as well as to the vote-getting effects of his efforts-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: And log-rolling.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Well, that is the word I was going to use, but I hesitated in these days of international peace to use such a word as that lest it might give offence to someone who was propounding doctrines of everlasting good will in Asia. So I merely content myself with saying that what I had in mind

Supply-Pensions-Appeal Court
was that with the exception of one country where a majority vote in congress carried a pension to an individual I know of no country in which it could be said that the right to secure a pension to a widow or anybody else on the basis of any claim that could be put forward should depend upon the judgment of the community in which the applicant lived. Human nature is sympathetic still, to its credit be it said, and I hope will long continue to be so. But if those charged with the unfortunate responsibility of administering a law are to be laid open to an attack upon their sympathetic natures, all we would have to do would be to induce the minister to believe that this would have a most potent effect upon the voting power of Quebec East, West, South or North at the next election, and sympathy would be so aroused that pensions would be granted to everyone.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I wish to thank the right hon. leader of the opposition for taking part in this discussion. He is a very able representative of the legal profession, a distinguished member of the bar. However, I should like to point out to him that in the court in which he has always practised he must prove his case beyond any reasonable doubt.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No; in a civil case by preponderance of testimony; in a criminal case beyond reasonable doubt.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is the case in the court in which the right hon. gentleman has practised. That is also the case in the court in which the president of the pension appeal court practised before he came over here. But our statute says that that benefit of the doubt clause shall not be interpreted in that way; that the benefit of the doubt must be given in favour of the applicant.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Of what doubt?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Let us come to the doubt. First, let me say a word about the two judges. I think very properly the right hon. gentleman referred to the pension appeal court judge as a man of experience and, as he says, a man of long standing at the bar. Then I asked the second simple question, I hope not an embarassing question, What did the right hon. gentleman think of Mr. Justice Taylor? If I caught the answer aright it was this, that he was also a very able legal gentleman but he was afraid that perhaps the heart got a little in advance of the head.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I did not express any opinion about Mr. Justice Taylor.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: You said he was a little warmer hearted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That he was a soldier.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Well, that is the inference I took. I take it that both of these men are skilled in the law. Now what does this benefit of the doubt clause say? I am going to read it once more:
. . . the body adjudicating on the claim shall be entitled to draw and shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences in favour of the applicant.
All reasonable inferences in favour of the applicant. I should like to ask this committee; I should like to ask any judge, Would it not be a reasonable inference that a man who was a cripple, who had an artificial leg, who, according to the evidence was careful, looked twice to the south, and who handicapped as he was had made the crossing with the exception of the last ten or twelve inches when the left mudguard of the car hit him, could, if he had had two good legs have made that other foot and been out of danger? Surely that is the way to interpret the benefit of the doubt clause in favour of the returned soldier.
I recognize very well that perhaps the minister has no jurisdiction. But when there is a wrong there must be a remedy. I am going to ask him once more to look into this case to see if there is not some way whereby what I think almost everyone will concede was an injustice, is righted.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Although I had never heard of the case mentioned by the hon. member for Saskatoon until to-night, I am particularly grateful that he has brought up this case, and grateful also for the comments of the right hon. leader of the opposition, because it gives me opportunity to say in this committee something which I have been aching to say long before I came to this house. Although I am not a lawyer I could not help feeling convinced as I listened to this discussion to-night that in this instance the court of appeal had brought to bear on this particular case every conceivable argument except the one which to me is most essential. And with no particular disrespect to the legal profession I would say that the appeal court have not shown themselves to possess the least commonly practised of all qualifications, the qualification of common sense. Neither am I a doctor. I have no desire to disparage the contributions that doctors and lawyers have made either to the country during the war or on behalf of returned men since the war. But in spite of those contributions I think they have been one of the returned men's most serious liabilities since the war. In spite of the fact that I am not a professional man I

Sup-ply-Pensions-Appeal Court
can think of these decisions, as well as any other hon. member perhaps, in terms of the men who are most interested in and most affected by them, the returned soldiers.
This is not a party question; it is not a question of this parliament or the last parliament. We have made much ado about the benefit of the doubt in all questions affecting the returned soldier, and the general consensus of opinion among the returned men is that it does not mean anything. The returned man puts it rather more profanely than I think the chairman would permit me to put it here. The reason it does not mean anything is that it can be explained away in terms of the law from every conceivable case where it might mean anything to the returned men.
By and large clause 73 does not mean anything. This type of example, which can be multiplied over and over again not only in the experience of the leader of the opposition but in the experience of the humblest member of this chamber, has caused this clause to become a joke. Having no knowledge of the merits of this case, but having listened to the hon. member for Saskatoon and to the learned, but from the standpoint of the returned soldier completely ineffective defence of the situation by the leader of the opposition, I am glad to have an opportunity to say that returned men in general figure that the benefit of the doubt clause does not mean anything. If we do nothing else in this session we ought either to define this clause to make it mean something or remove it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I have listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Saskatoon, the right hon. leader of the opposition and the hon. member for one of the Winnipegs. The hon. member for Winnipeg South said a few moments ago that he was neither a lawyer nor a doctor. The other evening I happened to be talking to him, out at his excellency's, and he told me that he was a curler, and that he had just returned from some part of Ontario where he had spent three, four or five enjoyable days. I was very glad that he had that pleasure, but when it comes to the returned soldiers and the legislation which is upon our statute books may I say, as I stated last year, that I had an opportunity of appearing before the appeal court, not for the purpose of presenting any argument but to accompany a gentleman from Halifax who, I believed, was entitled to consideration. After the argument had been heard Mr. Justice Hyndman, the chairman of the court, said to me, "'Mr. Finn, do you desire to make any statement?" I replied, "No, Mr. Chair-

man, I do not. I accompanied the gentleman from Halifax only in order that he might feel at home when bis case was being argued." Mr. Justice Hyndman replied, "I only wish that every hon. gentleman who sits in the House of Commons would come down with his constituents and at least give that moral support which is so necessary, even if they do not succeed."
I remember very well when I was studying law at Dalhousie university, of which the right hon. leader of the opposition is a graduate and to which he has been so financially kind. I remember that a fellow student in, I think it was, our second or final year, found himself faced with the question, What is the rule in Shelley's case? The gentleman who was not very studious was rather looking at the answers being written on foolscap by a fellow classmate who was studious, but with that the president of the university, the Reverend Doctor Forrest, came along, together with Professor McMechan, and this wonderful professor, the late Dean Weldon, was in the offing and therefore the student had no further opportunity of cribbing. He thought possibly it was a catch question, and after considering it for a while finally he made up his mind to answer it. The rule in Shelley's case, of course, which was settled by the House of Lords, was that a person could not devise or control his property "beyond a life or lives in being and twenty-one years." That is a settled principle; it applies to every person who has any wealth-and I do not think there is as much wealth on this side of the house as there is on the other.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
You are mistaken there.
Mr. FINN; I will say to my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, the exPrime Minister, that I had not him in mind. Rather I had in mind statements which appeared in the Citizen last evening in reference to the wealth which belonged to a gentleman who has passed on to "that bourne from which no traveller returns," who was highly respected in this house and in this country, and who has left a name that can be conjured with not only by this generation but by the generation which will read history in the light of his living and his passing.
In any case my friend the non-studious student thought he would make an attempt to answer the question, and he did so. He wrote down the question: What is the rule in Shelley's case? And then he said the answer was: "The rule in Shelley's case is the same as in any other man's case. Any d- fool ought to know that." The result was that he failed in more than two subjects and there-

Supply-Pensions-Appeal Court
fore lost his year. Professor George Ritchie, who was professor "of wills"-we used to call him "Svengali"-did not put him in to return for a supplementary in September but put him in to return at the opening of college to take a new year. It took him six years to get through, and he is not now practising his profession. So I think perhaps my hon. friend-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The hon. member should have said he was a judge.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No; I was speaking of Mr. Justice Hyndman as a judge but of the other gentleman as a fellow student and in my class at Dalhousie university, of which my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition is a graduate and of which he is very proud; and so am I. I think he has more reason to be proud than I have, because I was rather a bad boy in college and I have not lost all those qualities yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Was he not a bad boy in college?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Before my time. But, Mr. Chairman, I was going to say that I agree with the legal principle laid down by the right hon. leader of the opposition. It is not of a sympathetic character, not because he is not sympathetic but because the law must be interpreted as it has been placed upon the statute books. Therefore he is against the gentleman who had the wooden leg, and I do not say that unkindly or frivolously. The hon. member for Saskatoon can go home with the assurance that he has made the best of a bad case; and a wooden leg is the cause of the downfall.
Let me go further, and say that at the last session of parliament, when the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) was bringing down his estimates-and he has taken such an interest in his department, and is always available and sympathetic to the returned soldier; I know of no hon. gentleman in this house, whether he sits in opposition, or did, or sat on this side when they were here or sat over there when we were here- though I was never over there and I never expect to be-who ever made a greater success of his department.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Do you think it will be after the next election?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
All I can say to my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition is that he should have his horoscope read. I had mine read the other day. There were no politics in it, but it said I was too generous, too kind, too sympathetic, and worried too much. I think that also applies to the right 51D52-40
hon. gentleman, and that may be the reason he will come over here.
To resume, Mr. Chairman, last year I referred to a nurse at Camp Hill hospital. She had been overseas; she had served well, but she had arrived at the age of sixty-five. She was not entitled to pension on the ground of disability through being wounded or having a wooden leg; at least I do not think so. But, sir, she was a nurse, but had not the required time. She might have been on the Llandovery Castle, and if she had been she never would have returned to this country, any more than did Miss Fraser, who was also a nurse, the daughter of a late lieutenant governor of Nova Scotia, Hon. D. C. Fraser, who sat in this house and finally climaxed his honoured career by becoming lieutenant governor of his native province. I said last year, and I say again to-night, that in cases of this kind, where the pension granted is insufficient, the law should be elastic enough to permit action being taken. Some person should have authority where a strong equity is established, to deal with such cases.
In this instance the Minister of Pensions, through the officers of his department, saw his way clear to recommend the payment of a gratuity to help the nurse in the few years yet to be hers. I do suggest to the minister and to the government which, at the present time the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) is leading-and he will lead that day when he brings down the finest budget that has ever been brought down; I am giving away no government secrets, because I am not a member of the government; if I were I would not tell you-if legislation is to be brought down by the Minister of Pensions, provision should be made whereby all cases which have been adjudicated upon in the courts might be considered by the minister, or by some other persons indicated by parliament. But where there is a strong case in equity, as there was in this instance, certainly help should be given. Here we had a nurse who had served long and well, and yet at the age of sixty-five she found herself out in the cold and looking up at the citadel, thinking that while once the guns of that citadel belched forth, nothing was now belching forth from Camp Hill, not even a fifty cent piece.
It is fortunate that that case was dealt with, and I want to thank the minister for the way in which he acted. The nurse in question will have some comforts in the few years still left to her, and believe that she owes a debt of gratitude to the minister, to the government and to the house for that gratuity in dollars and cents which meant so much to her happiness of heart and mind.

Because, after all, when we begin to get "in the sere and yellow leaf" the finest qualities in the individual come out. I do not think anyone displays them more than the right hon. the leader of the opposition-and of course I do not suggest he is "in the sere and yellow leaf"; I think he is in the pink.
My other point was this: Last year I had in mind the case of an individual whose name I could not mention. He was a diffident chap living in the north end of the city of Halifax. He and his three brothers went overseas. His father, who is now dead, had served in the South African war. Each of his brothers was wounded three times, and he was wounded four times, the last wound being in the head. As a result of gas he developed a lung condition and to-day he is in the advanced stage of tuberculosis. That man receives $7.50 per month under the Pension Act, and was receiving from the city of Halifax an amount which brought him in a total of $18 per month. That money paid his board in a little dark room in the north end of the city.
I say to all hon. members, irrespective of party affiliation, that cases of this kind may be considered along with those mentioned by the leader of the opposition. He who deals with the law is a god, and therefore I would say that the Minister of Pensions should take these matters in a reflective mood, as together with his deputies he sits by the fireside trying to see if it is possible to work out a solution for such cases. It will not be very long before it will be de mortuis est with the soldiers to whom I refer, and then there will be no more opportunity. He will meet his God who, as was stated by the leader of the opposition, is a most just God, a most kind God and most charitable. I add the word "charitable," because charity covers a multitude of sins, and therefore I shall have to do a great deal of charity.
I shall be privileged to give a memorandum to the Minister of Pensions in order that he may be able to deal with this matter. Perhaps it may be the foundation stone by which a section of the amendment to the Pension Act will permit cases of that kind to be considered in a humane fashion.
I lost a nephew in the war, Lieutenant Clifford Finn, and I often think that the man who was best off is not the man, old or young, who was wounded, but the man who is over there beneath the poppies. He is better off than the man who lives to-day to whom little gratitude has been extended. He thinks that we in parliament are callous and cold when we are asked to consider the needs and

requirements of the homes and families of the returned men.
When the leader of the opposition spoke he was not sitting as a judge in the house, or one interpreting the statute. He was big and strong enough to state the facts, irrespective of a possible suggestion by someone in the west that he might not be sympathetic towards the soldiers. I do not believe that is his attitude, because I have some knowledge of the attitude of the right hon. gentleman. I know about his vast charities, and therefore I say a man of that type would not single out a returned soldier and say, No. to him, unless the courts were dead against him. He would be given a hearing, if he could prove his case "beyond a reasonable doubt."

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the observations of the leader of the opposition. As he has said, I think there are few in the house who do not know of cases similar to that set out by the hon. member for Saskatoon. I know of more than one. In my opinion the question with respect to the application of the clause dealing with the benefit of the doubt is a very important one.
For some years the manner in which this provision has been applied, and the results secured, have been difficult to understand. The inference permitted to be drawn seems to be an inference of fact, something which is left for the trial tribunal to decide. If first the pension commission and then the quorum, or perhaps several commission hearings and one or two quorum hearings, exercising that privilege they have of drawing inferences of fact, are unanimous in finding that there is a doubt and that the applicant is entitled to the benefit of that doubt, then I do not see how the appellate tribunal can find that there is not sufficient doubt and overrule the decision in favour of the applicant.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Would it interfere with my hon. friend if I put it in this way: In this case there was no evidence upon which an inference could be drawn. That is what the appellate court said.
. Mr. HAMILTON: I had thought of that but according to the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) there was apparently certain evidence given at the inquest as to where the body lay, how far it was away and where the tracks of the car were from which an inference might have been permitted to be drawn. If there is an exercise of the power to draw inferences from facts; if the appeal is dealt with as a matter of law and not as a matter of fact, where there has been so many decisions, either majority or

Questions
unanimous, of trial tribunals in favour of giving the benefit of the doubt to the appellant, then it is difficult for me to see how the appellate tribunal can overrule them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
knows that there are many cases in which juries find certain verdicts and the courts set them aside because there was no evidence upon which the findings could be made. That is the real point of this case.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I appreciate that. They cannot make a finding on the facts on the ground that the finding would be perverse or something.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No evidence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No evidence of a type upon which a finding could be made. In overruling the decisions of whatever tribunals there may be I am not sure that the court of appeal is not exercising the functions that should be properly exercised by the quorums. They are overruling the doubt which has been found in favour of the appellant. The appeal tribunal is saying that despite the fact that it has been found that there is a doubt, in their estimation that doubt does not exist. That overruling is confined to the applying of principles of law, such as the right hon. leader of the opposition has suggested. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) that there is a feeling throughout the country that the benefit of the doubt clause does not operate fairly in favour of applicants making application for pensions.
